Parvi v. City of Kingston (N.Y. 1977) — consciousness of confinement

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.D

Facts: Two Kingston police officers found Parvi, who was drunk, in a downtown alley. He told them he had nowhere to go, so they drove him to an abandoned golf course outside the city to "dry out" and left him. He wandered onto the New York State Thruway and was hit by a car. At trial he said he could not remember whether he had been aware of being confined. The trial court dismissed his false imprisonment claim.

Held: Fuchsberg, J.: in New York, false imprisonment, a dignitary tort, requires that the plaintiff be conscious of the confinement. But a present memory of that awareness is not required. Alcohol or his injuries may have erased the memory, and other evidence could show he was aware at the time. Reversed.

Why it matters: Under the dignitary-tort view, the plaintiff must know of the confinement or be harmed by it (R2d § 42).

Dissent (Breitel, C.J.): Parvi remembered nothing and knew of the incident only from later conversations, so he did not make out a prima facie case.

main case

Hardy v. LaBelle's Distributing Co. (Mont. 1983) — voluntary submission

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.D

Facts: Hardy, a temporary employee, was asked to "tour" the store and was taken into the manager's office, where other employees and a uniformed police officer were present. She was told she had been accused of stealing a watch. She denied it, agreed to take a lie detector test, passed, and received an apology. She testified that she felt she could not leave but that she stayed voluntarily to clear her name. The jury found for LaBelle's.

Held: False imprisonment is the unlawful restraint of a person against her will. Hardy admitted she wanted to stay to exonerate herself, and no threats or force kept her there. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Restraint against the plaintiff's will is required. Staying to protect one's reputation is not confinement.

main case

Enright v. Groves (Colo. App. 1977) — false arrest

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.D

Facts: Officer Groves saw a dog running loose in violation of the Fort Collins leash ordinance. Mrs. Enright's 11-year-old son said it was his dog and that his mother was in a car at the curb. Groves demanded Mrs. Enright's driver's license. She gave her name and address but refused to produce the license. He told her to produce it or go to jail; she said "Isn't this ridiculous?" and he arrested her. She was later convicted of the leash violation, and a jury awarded her $1,500 for false imprisonment.

Held: Probable cause, or a conviction for the offense for which the person was arrested, defeats a false arrest claim. But Groves arrested Enright for failing to produce her license, not for the leash violation, and no law required a person who was not driving to produce a license on demand. Groves had no authority to make the arrest. Affirmed.

Why it matters: False arrest is false imprisonment under asserted legal authority. Justification depends on the offense for which the person was actually arrested.

main case

Whittaker v. Sandford (Me. 1912) — confinement by refusing release

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.D

Facts: Whittaker had been a member of a religious sect abroad led by Sandford. She decided to leave and accepted his offer of passage home to America on his yacht, on his promise that she would not be detained on board, especially not to reconvert her. When the yacht reached port, Sandford refused to provide a boat to take her ashore, and she was kept on the yacht for about a month, though she was otherwise free to move about it.

Held: Savage, J.: false imprisonment does not require laying hands on the plaintiff; it is enough that her freedom of movement is restrained. When the defendant has a duty to provide a means of release, as Sandford did here by his promise and control of the boats, refusing to do so is an imprisonment. The verdict was upheld on liability.

Why it matters: An omission counts when there is a duty to release (R2d § 45). Compare the general no-duty-to-act rule in negligence (§ 21).

note

Shopkeeper's privilege and other justifications are in § 9 (Bonkowski) and § 10 (Sindle). Treat them as defenses after you have set out the prima facie case.

sections.title: 5. Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress
sections.html:
rule

IIED: R2d § 46(1); Harris v. Jones

The defendant is liable when all required:
(1) the conduct is intentional or reckless;
(2) the conduct is extreme and outrageous;
(3) the conduct causes the emotional distress; and
(4) the distress is severe.

  • Outrageous means "so outrageous in character, and so extreme in degree, as to go beyond all possible bounds of decency," so that "atrocious" is the community's reaction (R2d § 46 cmt. d). Mere insults, indignities, threats, annoyances, and petty oppressions are not enough.
  • Factors pointing to outrageousness weighed together:
    (1) abuse of a position of power or authority, such as an employer, police officer, landlord, or collection agency;
    (2) knowledge of the plaintiff's special susceptibility;
    (3) repeated conduct or a campaign of harassment;
    (4) threats of violence; and
    (5) public humiliation or racial or other identity-based abuse.
  • Recklessness: the defendant acts in deliberate disregard of a high probability that distress will follow.
  • Severe: distress no reasonable person could be expected to endure. Physical symptoms are not required but help prove it. The intensity and duration of the distress count.
  • Common carriers and innkeepers are traditionally liable for gross insults to passengers and guests even without outrageousness (Slocum discusses this exception).
main case

State Rubbish Collectors Ass'n v. Siliznoff (Cal. 1952) — recognizing the tort

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.E

Facts: Siliznoff took over collecting rubbish from a brewery that an association member claimed. Association officers told him he had to join and pay, or they would beat him up, destroy his truck, and put him out of business. He signed notes to pay the association, then refused to pay. The association sued on the notes, and he cross-claimed for the distress the threats caused; he testified he was so frightened he became ill, vomited, and missed work. The jury found for Siliznoff.

Held: Traynor, J.: one who, without privilege, intentionally causes severe emotional distress by outrageous conduct is liable, even without physical injury and even though the threats of future harm were not an assault. Mental suffering is already compensated as part of assault, battery, and false imprisonment, so it is anomalous to deny it standing alone. Affirmed.

Why it matters: This case established IIED as a stand-alone tort. Physical injury is not required.

main case

Slocum v. Food Fair Stores of Florida (Fla. 1958) — mere insults

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.E

Facts: Slocum asked a Food Fair employee the price of an item. He replied, "If you want to know the price, you'll have to find out the best way you can... you stink to me." She said the shock brought on a heart attack. The trial court dismissed her complaint.

Held: There is no liability for mere insults, indignities, or threats, whatever their consequences. An ordinary person would suffer only slight distress from this remark, and the special liability of common carriers and innkeepers for insulting patrons does not extend to a grocery store. Making trivial insults actionable would also chill speech. Affirmed.

Why it matters: This sets the floor: rudeness is not outrageous, and the plaintiff's unknown susceptibility does not make it so.

main case

Harris v. Jones (Md. 1977) — the four elements; severity

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.E

Facts: Harris, a General Motors employee, had stuttered all his life and was nervous about it. His supervisor, Jones, knowing this, mimicked and ridiculed his stutter about 30 times over five months. Harris said this made him more nervous and worsened his stutter. The jury found for Harris against Jones and GM, but the trial court granted judgment notwithstanding the verdict.

Held: Murphy, C.J.: Maryland recognizes IIED with four elements: (1) intentional or reckless conduct; (2) extreme and outrageous conduct; (3) causation; and (4) severe distress. Jones's conduct, knowing Harris's susceptibility, satisfied the first three, but Harris failed on severity. His stutter and nervousness predated the abuse, and he offered no evidence of how much worse they became. Affirmed.

Why it matters: This is the elements case. Severity is a real hurdle, and a supervisor's power and knowledge of a susceptibility go to outrageousness, not severity.

rule

IIED aimed at a third person: R2d § 46(2)

When outrageous conduct is directed at a third person, the actor is liable if he intentionally or recklessly causes severe emotional distress any one suffices: (a) to a member of that person's immediate family who is present at the time, whether or not the distress results in bodily harm; or (b) to any other person who is present at the time, if the distress results in bodily harm.

Most courts also require that the defendant know the plaintiff is present (Taylor).

main case

Taylor v. Vallelunga (Cal. App. 1959) — bystander IIED: presence known

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.E

Facts: Vallelunga beat Taylor's father. Taylor watched the beating and suffered severe emotional distress. Her complaint did not allege that Vallelunga knew she was present or intended to distress her. The trial court sustained a demurrer.

Held: A plaintiff who witnesses an attack on a family member recovers for her own distress only if the defendant knew she was present, so that he intended, or was substantially certain, to cause her distress. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Intent does not transfer into IIED. Knowledge of the bystander's presence takes its place.

note

Bias lens and limits

  • Racial slurs by an employer or supervisor can be outrageous because of the power imbalance and the history the words carry (Alcorn v. Anbro Engineering, Cal. 1970). Compare Fisher (§ 3), which used battery.
  • The First Amendment limits IIED for speech on public matters: public figures must prove actual malice (Hustler Magazine v. Falwell, 1988), and speech on public issues in a public place is protected (Snyder v. Phelps, 2011).
exam tips

IIED often comes up as a backup claim. Ask first whether a traditional tort (assault, battery, false imprisonment) fits. Then argue outrageousness with the factors and confront severity directly. Graders look for both elements.

sections.title: 6. Trespass to Land, Trespass to Chattels, and Conversion
sections.html:
rule

Trespass to land: R2d § 158

One who intentionally does any of the following is liable, whether or not harm results any one suffices:
(a) enters land in the possession of another, or causes a thing or a third person to do so;
(b) remains on the land; or
(c) fails to remove from the land a thing which he is under a duty to remove.

  • Intent means intent to enter the land, not intent to trespass. Believing in good faith that the land is your own is no defense (compare Ranson). An involuntary entry, such as being thrown onto the land, is not a trespass.
  • No damage needed (Dougherty). Nominal damages are available, and the actor is liable for any harm the intrusion causes, even if it was unforeseeable and caused without negligence.
  • Airspace and subsurface. The possessor owns the space above the land within the zone of reasonable use, and the area beneath it (Herrin). Aircraft overflights in navigable airspace are privileged (United States v. Causby, 1946).
  • Continuing trespass: staying, or leaving a thing on the land, after permission ends is a trespass (Rogers; R2d § 160).
  • Unintended intrusions that are negligent or reckless are governed by negligence and require actual harm (R2d § 165).
  • Plaintiff: the person in possession, such as a tenant, not necessarily the owner.
main case

Dougherty v. Stepp (N.C. 1835) — no damage required

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.F

Facts: Stepp entered Dougherty's land without permission and surveyed part of it with a surveyor's chain, claiming it as his own. He marked no trees and cut no brush. The jury found for Stepp, apparently because there was no damage.

Held: Ruffin, C.J.: every unauthorized entry on another's land is a trespass, whether or not it causes actual damage. The law infers damage, "if nothing more, the treading down the grass or herbage." Reversed; new trial ordered.

Why it matters: Trespass protects the right to exclude. Nominal damages vindicate the right and can establish title.

main case

Herrin v. Sutherland (Mont. 1925) — shooting over land

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.F

Facts: While hunting, Sutherland repeatedly fired his shotgun at ducks and other birds flying over Herrin's land, over his house and cattle. The shot did not land on the property, but the firing disturbed Herrin's quiet enjoyment.

Held: Callaway, C.J.: firing through the airspace close to the surface is a trespass, though nothing touched the ground. A possessor's rights extend to the airspace he may reasonably use, and missiles crossing it endanger people and property. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Intrusions into the airspace near the ground are trespasses.

main case

Rogers v. Board of Road Comm'rs for Kent County (Mich. 1947) — continuing trespass after a license

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.F

Facts: The Board had a license to put up a snow fence on the Rogers farm each winter, on the condition that it remove the fence, posts included, at the end of each season. It left an anchor post in the ground. The next summer, Rogers's husband was mowing the field when his mower hit the post; he was thrown off and killed. The trial court dismissed the complaint.

Held: Reid, J.: once the license expired, leaving the post on the land was a trespass, and the Board is liable for the resulting harm whether or not it was negligent. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: R2d § 158(c): a lawful entry becomes a trespass when the duty to remove arises, and liability extends to the consequences.

rule

Trespass by airborne particles: Bradley; Borland v. Sanders Lead (Ala. 1979)

An invasion by microscopic airborne particles is a trespass only if all required:
(1) it is an invasion affecting an interest in the exclusive possession of property;
(2) the defendant intentionally did the act that resulted in the invasion;
(3) it was reasonably foreseeable that the act could result in an invasion of the plaintiff's possessory interest; and
(4) the property (the res) suffered substantial damage.

If the particles cause no damage to the land itself, the claim is in nuisance (§ 33), which requires a substantial interference with use and enjoyment.

main case

Bradley v. American Smelting & Refining Co. (W.D. Wash. 1986) — particle trespass needs damage to the land

Source: Canvas reading (9/8), from the opinion text in the course folder.

Facts: The Bradleys owned land on the southern end of Vashon Island, about four miles north of ASARCO's copper smelter at Ruston, Washington. For years the smelter emitted particles of arsenic and cadmium that the wind carried onto their land; the particles were imperceptible to human senses. The Bradleys sued in trespass and nuisance. The federal court certified questions to the Washington Supreme Court, which held (104 Wash. 2d 677 (1985)) that intentionally emitting imperceptible pollutants that settle on another's land may be a trespass as well as a nuisance; that such a trespass requires proof of actual and substantial damages; and that the three-year trespass limitations period applies. Back in federal court, soil from the Bradleys' garden showed 53 ppm arsenic and 1.7 ppm cadmium, above normal background levels. ASARCO's experts said these levels posed no danger. The Bradleys offered no evidence of actual harm or of lost property value, only their worry about health risks.

Held: Rothstein, J.: summary judgment for ASARCO. Trespass: under the test the Washington Supreme Court adopted from Borland, the plaintiff must show substantial damage to the land. Without that rule, "every landowner within a hundred miles of a manufacturing plant" could sue. The evidence showed the particles had not harmed the land, and claimed loss of value was unsupported. Nuisance: the plaintiff must show substantial interference with use and enjoyment. Worry about a health risk the evidence shows does not exist is not enough, because distress counts in nuisance only if it causes physical symptoms or accompanies an actual or threatened invasion of the plaintiff's person or security. Action dismissed.

Why it matters: The modern rule for pollution trespass. Trespass protects exclusive possession and does not ask whether the defendant acted reasonably, so courts require real damage to the land before treating invisible particles as a trespass. Otherwise the claim belongs in nuisance, which balances reasonableness.

rule

Trespass to chattels: R2d §§ 217–218

Conduct any one suffices: the actor intentionally (a) dispossesses another of the chattel; or (b) uses or intermeddles with a chattel in the possession of another.

Liability, beyond nominal damages, only if any one suffices:
(a) the possessor is dispossessed;
(b) the chattel is impaired as to its condition, quality, or value;
(c) the possessor is deprived of the use of the chattel for a substantial time; or
(d) bodily harm is caused to the possessor, or harm is caused to some person or thing in which the possessor has a legally protected interest.

main case

Glidden v. Szybiak (N.H. 1949) — harmless intermeddling

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.G

Facts: Four-year-old Elaine Glidden climbed on the Szybiaks' dog, Toby, on the porch of a store and pulled its ears. The dog bit her. A New Hampshire statute made dog owners liable for bites unless the victim was committing "a trespass or other tort." The owner argued Elaine had committed a trespass to the dog.

Held: Branch, C.J.: harmless intermeddling with a chattel is not actionable. A trespass to chattels requires actual damage to the chattel or deprivation of its use, and there was no evidence the dog was harmed. Because Elaine committed no tort, the statutory defense failed and she could recover.

Why it matters: R2d § 218: harmless meddling with a chattel is not actionable, unlike trespass to land.

main case

CompuServe Inc. v. Cyber Promotions, Inc. (S.D. Ohio 1997) — spam as trespass to chattels

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.G

Facts: Cyber Promotions sent unsolicited email advertisements to CompuServe's subscribers by the millions. CompuServe told it to stop and installed filters; Cyber increased its volume and falsified the return information to get past the filters. CompuServe sought a preliminary injunction on a trespass to chattels theory.

Held: Graham, J.: electronic signals sent to a computer system can be a use of or intermeddling with a chattel (R2d § 217(b)). Harm was shown: (1) the volume burdened CompuServe's processing power and disk space, diminishing the equipment's value (§ 218(b)); and (2) subscribers complained and canceled, harming CompuServe's goodwill and business interests (§ 218(d)). Cyber's First Amendment defense failed because CompuServe is a private actor. Preliminary injunction granted.

Why it matters: The old tort applied to new technology, though actual harm is still required. Intel Corp. v. Hamidi (Cal. 2003) found no harm from a few emails.

sections.title: Conversion (the casebook's next section; not on the syllabus pages)
sections.html:
rule

Conversion: R2d § 222A

Conversion is an intentional exercise of dominion or control over a chattel that so seriously interferes with another's right to control it that the actor may justly be required to pay its full value.

Seriousness factors weighed together:
(a) the extent and duration of the actor's exercise of dominion or control;
(b) the actor's intent to assert a right in fact inconsistent with the other's right of control;
(c) the actor's good faith;
(d) the extent and duration of the resulting interference with the other's right of control;
(e) the harm done to the chattel; and
(f) the inconvenience and expense caused to the other.

note case

Pearson v. Dodd (D.C. Cir. 1969) — copying information is not conversion

Source: 13th ed. Ch. 2.H (pages the syllabus skips)

Facts: Two former members of Senator Dodd's staff, aided by two current members, entered his office at night without authority, removed documents from his files, photocopied them, and put the originals back. They gave the copies to columnists Drew Pearson and Jack Anderson, who knew how they had been obtained and published articles based on them. The district court granted Dodd partial summary judgment on conversion.

Held: J. Skelly Wright, J.: there was no conversion. The originals were returned before they were missed, so Dodd was not deprived of them. The information itself was not literary property, a scientific invention, or a secret business plan, the kinds of information the law protects as property. Reversed.

Why it matters: Conversion protects tangible things and a few forms of intellectual property. The remedy for publishing information is privacy or defamation law.

Trespass to chattels

Conversion

Interference

Minor: use, intermeddling, short dispossession

Serious: destroying, keeping, selling, major alteration

Damages

Actual harm or loss of use (no nominal damages without harm)

Full value at the time of conversion, a forced sale

Good faith

Irrelevant to liability

Irrelevant to liability, but a factor in seriousness

Example

Moving a car to another space

Stealing it, or wrecking it while joyriding

sections.title: 7. Consent
sections.html:
rule

When consent is a defense

Consent bars an intentional tort claim when all required:
(1) the plaintiff had the capacity to consent;
(2) the plaintiff consented, actually or apparently, to the defendant's conduct or to substantially the same conduct;
(3) the consent was not procured by fraud about an essential matter or by duress; and
(4) the defendant stayed within the scope of the consent.

  • Forms of consent any one suffices:
    • (1) Express, in words or writing;
    • (2) Implied in fact, or apparent: the plaintiff's conduct reasonably appears to show consent, judged objectively (O'Brien). Silence counts where a reasonable person would object if unwilling.
    • (3) Implied by custom: the ordinary contacts of social life and the rules of a game (Wallace, Hackbart).
    • (4) Implied by law: in an emergency, when the person cannot consent, a reasonable person would consent, and the actor has no reason to think this person would refuse (R2d § 892D).
  • Capacity. Children, intoxicated people, and people with significant cognitive impairments may lack capacity. A parent or guardian can consent for them.
  • Fraud about the essential character of the act, not just a collateral matter, vitiates consent (De May; R2d § 892B(2)). A lie about collateral matters, such as payment, does not.
  • Consent to a crime. The majority view is that consent to a criminal act, such as an illegal boxing match or a mutual fight, is ineffective, so each participant can sue. R2d § 892C makes consent effective unless the statute was meant to protect a class from its own poor judgment, as with statutory rape and child-labor laws.
  • Burden: consent is usually an affirmative defense, but for offensive battery its absence is often treated as part of the plaintiff's case.
main case

O'Brien v. Cunard S.S. Co. (Mass. 1891) — consent shown by conduct

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.A

Facts: To spare passengers quarantine on arrival in Boston, Cunard vaccinated immigrants on board against smallpox and posted notices in several languages. O'Brien stood in line with about 200 women. The surgeon examined her arm, said there was no vaccination mark, and she held up her arm and was vaccinated without objecting. She later claimed she had been vaccinated before, did not want it, and suffered ulceration from the vaccine.

Held: Knowlton, J.: consent is judged by the plaintiff's outward conduct. A surgeon may act on what a person's behavior shows, and her standing in line and holding up her arm, without objecting, showed consent. Verdict for Cunard affirmed.

Why it matters: Consent is judged objectively: the defendant may rely on outward manifestations. Note the power imbalance, though. Immigrants needed vaccination to land.

main case

Hackbart v. Cincinnati Bengals, Inc. (10th Cir. 1979) — consent in sports

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.A

Facts: During a regular season game, Bengals fullback Charles "Booby" Clark, frustrated after a play had ended, struck Broncos safety Dale Hackbart on the back of the head with his forearm while Hackbart was kneeling. Hackbart suffered a serious neck fracture. The trial court ruled that professional football is so violent that tort law does not reach blows between players.

Held: Doyle, J.: players consent to contact within the rules and customs of the game, not to an intentional blow the rules prohibit, struck in anger after the play. The NFL rules forbid striking an opponent on the head with a forearm. Liability can rest on intentional or reckless conduct. Reversed for a new trial.

Why it matters: Consent is limited to the risks inherent in the activity, as defined by its rules and customs. Violations outside the game support liability for intentional or reckless conduct.

main case

Mohr v. Williams (Minn. 1905) — exceeding the scope of consent

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.A

Facts: Mohr consented to an operation on her right ear. Once she was anesthetized, Dr. Williams found the right ear less serious than he had thought and, on examining the left ear, found it diseased and more in need of surgery. Without waking her, he operated on the left ear, successfully. She sued for battery. The jury awarded $14,322.50, but the trial judge granted a new trial as excessive. Both sides appealed.

Held: Brown, J.: operating on a different part of the body than the one consented to is a battery, however skillful or beneficial. A surgeon may go beyond the consent only if he finds, during the authorized operation, a condition that endangers life or health and requires immediate action. The left ear was not discovered during the authorized operation, and its condition was not an emergency. The order for a new trial (on damages) was affirmed.

Why it matters: Medical consent covers only the procedure authorized. Many courts now allow reasonable extensions of an operation when a condition is found under anesthesia and immediate action is in the patient's interest (Kennedy v. Parrott, N.C. 1956).

main case

De May v. Roberts (Mich. 1881) — consent procured by deceit

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.A

Facts: Dr. De May attended Mrs. Roberts in childbirth at her home. He brought with him Scattergood, a young unmarried man with no medical training, whom the Robertses took to be the doctor's assistant. Scattergood stayed throughout the delivery and held Mrs. Roberts's hand during a contraction.

Held: Marston, C.J.: consent obtained by deceit about a material fact is no consent. Mrs. Roberts allowed Scattergood's presence and touch only because she believed he was a medical assistant. Both De May and Scattergood are liable. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Fraud about the essential nature of the act or the actor vitiates consent. The case is also an ancestor of the privacy tort.

sections.title: Medical consent: battery or negligence?
sections.html:
Problem

Claim

Why

No consent at all, or a substantially different procedure (Mohr)

Battery

An unconsented touching; no expert testimony needed

Consent to the procedure, but material risks were not disclosed (Scott v. Bradford, § 13)

Negligence (informed consent)

A breach of the duty to disclose; causation must be shown

Consent obtained by lying about who will operate ("ghost surgery")

Battery

Fraud about an essential matter

sections.title: 8. Self-Defense and Defense of Others
sections.html:
rule

Self-defense: R2d §§ 63–65

The actor is privileged to use force when all required:
(1) the actor reasonably believes that another is about to inflict a harmful or offensive contact or confinement on him;
(2) the threat is imminent, not past or future; and
(3) the force used is reasonably necessary and proportionate to the threat.

Deadly force (force likely to cause death or serious bodily harm) is privileged only if the actor reasonably believes he faces death or serious bodily harm.

  • Reasonable mistake preserves the privilege. The test is whether a reasonable person would have believed force was needed. In Courvoisier v. Raymond (Colo. 1896), a store owner who shot a deputy sheriff, mistaking him for one of a rioting crowd, was entitled to an instruction on reasonable appearances.
  • Retreat. Under R2d § 65, before using deadly force, the actor must retreat if he can do so in complete safety, except in his own dwelling. Many states impose no duty to retreat, and stand-your-ground statutes eliminate it outside the home. No one must retreat before using non-deadly force.
  • Words alone never justify force. Neither does revenge for a completed attack.
  • Excessive force: the defender is liable for the excess, and the original aggressor may then defend himself against it.
  • Injury to a bystander: a defender who injures a third person while acting in privileged self-defense is liable only if he was negligent toward that person (R2d § 75). Transferred intent does not apply.
rule

Defense of others: R2d § 76

The actor may use the same force to defend a third person that he could use to defend himself when all required: (1) the actor reasonably believes that the third person would be privileged to defend himself; and (2) the actor reasonably believes that his intervention is necessary to protect the third person.

Mistake: the modern majority (and R2d) protects a reasonable mistake. The older rule put the intervenor "in the shoes" of the person defended, so he was liable if that person was actually the aggressor.

exam tips

For any privilege, separate the elements:
(1) the belief;
(2) whether it was reasonable;
(3) imminence; and
(4) proportionality. Most exam answers turn on proportionality, such as deadly force against a non-deadly threat, or on the timing of force used after the threat ended.

sections.title: 9. Defense and Recovery of Property; the Shopkeeper's Privilege
sections.html:
rule

Defense of property: R2d §§ 77, 79, 85

A possessor may use force to prevent or end an intrusion onto land or chattels when all required:
(1) the intrusion is not privileged;
(2) the possessor reasonably believes force is necessary to prevent or end it;
(3) the possessor first asks the intruder to desist, unless asking would be futile or dangerous; and
(4) the force is reasonable. Force intended or likely to cause death or serious bodily harm is never privileged to protect property alone.

  • Mechanical devices (spring guns, traps) are privileged only to the extent the possessor could have used the same force in person, and only if a warning is given where needed (R2d § 85). A device cannot tell a burglar from a child or a firefighter.
  • Mistake: unlike self-defense, a mistaken belief that the intruder is not privileged generally does not protect the defender, unless the intruder caused the mistake.
  • Defense of the dwelling against someone threatening the occupants is governed by self-defense, so deadly force may be justified by a threat to people, not by the intrusion itself.
main case

Katko v. Briney (Iowa 1971) — spring guns

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.D

Facts: The Brineys owned an unoccupied, boarded-up farmhouse that had been broken into repeatedly. They rigged a 20-gauge shotgun in a bedroom to fire at the legs of anyone who opened the door, and posted no warning. Katko broke in to steal old bottles and fruit jars. When he opened the bedroom door, the blast tore away much of his leg. He had pleaded guilty to larceny. The jury awarded $20,000 in actual and $10,000 in punitive damages.

Held: Moore, C.J.: a possessor may not use, to protect property alone, force or a device intended to kill or seriously injure an intruder. Such force is justified only when the intruder is committing a violent felony or endangering human life. The law values human life and limb above property, even a trespasser's who is committing a crime. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Human life and limb outweigh property interests. The force allowed through a device is no more than the possessor could use in person.

Dissent (Larson, J.): the jury should have been told it could find the gun was set only to frighten, the rule had never been applied to a burglar, and punitive damages should not be awarded to a plaintiff engaged in crime.

rule

Recovery of chattels: Hodgeden; R2d §§ 100–106

An owner may use reasonable force to recover a chattel when all required:
(1) the owner was wrongfully dispossessed, by force, fraud, or theft (not merely a debtor's failure to return it);
(2) the owner acts in fresh pursuit, promptly after discovering the taking;
(3) the owner first demands its return, unless a demand would be futile or dangerous; and
(4) the force used is reasonable and not likely to cause serious bodily harm.

main case

Hodgeden v. Hubbard (Vt. 1846) — fresh-pursuit recapture

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.E

Facts: Hodgeden bought a stove from the Hubbards on credit, misrepresenting his finances. Discovering the fraud almost at once, they rode after him and overtook him a few miles away. When he refused to return the stove and drew a knife, one of them held him while the other took the stove. Hodgeden sued for assault and battery and won below.

Held: Williams, C.J.: an owner who has been defrauded of goods may retake them by force if he acts without unreasonable delay and uses no unnecessary violence. The wrongdoer has no privilege to resist, and if he does, the owner may use the force needed to protect himself. Reversed.

Why it matters: Self-help recapture is allowed only in fresh pursuit and with reasonable force. Later, the owner must go to court.

rule

Shopkeeper's privilege: R2d § 120A; Bonkowski

A merchant may detain a person when all required:
(1) the merchant reasonably believes the person has taken, or is taking, goods without paying;
(2) the detention is on the premises or in their immediate vicinity;
(3) the detention is for a reasonable time and only to investigate; and
(4) the detention is carried out in a reasonable manner, with no more force than is reasonably necessary.

Most states codify the privilege. In Delaware, see 11 Del. C. § 840 (detention of suspected shoplifters).

main case

Bonkowski v. Arlan's Department Store (Mich. App. 1968) — merchant detention

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.E

Facts: As Mrs. Bonkowski walked to her car after leaving the store, a store security guard stopped her outside, said someone had told him she had taken costume jewelry, and told her to empty her purse. She did so on a ledge outside the store and showed receipts for her items; he let her go. She claimed psychological harm. The jury awarded her $43,750.

Held: Fitzgerald, J.: a merchant who reasonably believes a person has taken goods without paying may detain her for a reasonable investigation, in a reasonable manner, on or in the immediate vicinity of the premises. The jury should have been told about this privilege. Reversed and remanded for a new trial.

Why it matters: The privilege resolves the merchant's dilemma of letting a suspected thief go or risking false imprisonment liability.

note

Bias lens

The shopkeeper's privilege turns on "reasonable" suspicion. Studies and litigation show that store detentions fall disproportionately on Black shoppers ("shopping while Black"). Ask on the essay whether the grounds for suspicion were particular to the plaintiff, and whether the manner of detention was reasonable.

sections.title: 10. Necessity and Discipline
sections.html:
Public necessity (Surocco; R2d § 196)

Private necessity (Vincent; R2d § 197)

When

The actor reasonably believes it necessary to avert an imminent public disaster, such as fire, flood, or epidemic

The actor reasonably believes it necessary to protect his own or a third person's person or property from serious harm

Privilege

Complete: no liability for the harm

Incomplete: privileged to enter and use, but liable for actual damage

Owner's resistance

The owner may not resist

The owner may not resist or expel. An owner who does is liable (Ploof v. Putnam, Vt. 1908: unmooring a boat in a storm)

Compensation

None from the actor. A taking claim against the government may lie.

The actor pays for the damage caused

main case

Surocco v. Geary (Cal. 1853) — public necessity

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.F

Facts: During the great San Francisco fire of 1849, Geary, the alcalde, ordered Surocco's house blown up with gunpowder to stop the fire from spreading. Surocco was removing goods at the time and said he could have saved more of them if not for the blast. The trial court found for Surocco.

Held: Murray, C.J.: destroying private property to stop a conflagration is privileged by public necessity, if done in good faith under apparent necessity. No action lies against the person who did it, even if the property would have been saved, because otherwise no one would act to save the community. Reversed.

Why it matters: The community's safety outweighs one owner's property. The privilege is complete. Whether the destruction was actually necessary is judged by the circumstances at the time.

main case

Vincent v. Lake Erie Transp. Co. (Minn. 1910) — private necessity: pay for the damage

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.F

Facts: The steamship Reynolds was unloading at Vincent's dock in Duluth when a violent storm arose. The crew kept the ship moored to the dock overnight, replacing lines as they broke. The waves threw the ship against the dock, causing $500 of damage. The jury found for Vincent.

Held: O'Brien, J.: the ship was privileged by private necessity to stay at the dock, and keeping it there was prudent seamanship, not negligence. But a party who deliberately uses another's property to save his own must pay for the damage caused. Affirmed.

Why it matters: This is the incomplete privilege: an act can be both justified and compensable. The dissent would have treated the damage as a risk of the dock owner's business.

Dissent (Lewis, J.): the ship was lawfully at the dock and could not safely leave; the damage was an inevitable accident, and the dock owner, who invited the ship for profit, should bear the risk.

rule

Discipline and authority of law

Discipline: a parent, a person in loco parentis, or a teacher may use reasonable force, or confinement, reasonably believed necessary to control, train, or educate a child (R2d §§ 147–155). Reasonableness considers weighed together:
(1) the child's age, sex, and condition;
(2) the nature of the offense and the child's motive;
(3) the influence of the child's example on others;
(4) whether the force is necessary and appropriate to compel obedience; and
(5) whether it is disproportionate or likely to cause serious harm.

Restraint to protect people or property: reasonable detention, in time and manner, to prevent another from injuring people or damaging property in one's lawful custody is not unlawful (Sindle).

main case

Sindle v. New York City Transit Authority (N.Y. 1973) — justification for detention

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.G

Facts: Students on a school bus run by the Transit Authority became unruly and vandalized it. The driver, Mooney, warned them, then locked the doors, skipped the remaining stops, and drove toward the police station. Sindle, 14, jumped out of a window to escape and was run over by the rear wheels. At trial he waived his negligence claim, and the judge refused to let the defendants plead justification and excluded evidence of it. The jury awarded damages for false imprisonment.

Held: Jasen, J.: refusing leave to plead justification was an abuse of discretion; the defendants had the burden of proving it, and Sindle could not have been prejudiced. A restraint reasonable in time and manner, imposed to prevent injury to persons or damage to property in one's lawful custody, is not unlawful. The driver, entrusted with both the students and the bus, stood in a position like a teacher in loco parentis. Whether his detention was reasonable was for the jury. Reversed; new trial.

Why it matters: Justification is a defense to false imprisonment, but its reasonableness is a fact question. Detaining every passenger, including the innocent, presses the limits.

note

Arrest without a warrant (background)

  • A police officer may arrest without a warrant for a felony if he reasonably believes one was committed and that the arrestee committed it. A private citizen is privileged only if a felony was in fact committed and he reasonably believes the arrestee committed it.
  • For a misdemeanor, an arrest without a warrant generally requires a breach of the peace committed in the arrester's presence. See Enright (§ 4): the justification must fit the offense for which the person was actually arrested.
roadmap

Intentional torts and privileges: the week 5 MC checklist

1. Tort. Name each act and match it to a tort: contact (battery), apprehension (assault), confinement (false imprisonment), outrageous conduct (IIED), land (trespass), chattel (trespass to chattels or conversion).

2. Intent. Purpose or substantial certainty? Transferred between people or torts? Child, mental illness, or mistake does not defeat it.

3. Element traps. Awareness (needed for assault and, usually, false imprisonment; not for battery), imminence, reasonable means of escape, severity of distress, actual harm for chattels.

4. Privilege. Consent (scope, fraud, capacity), self-defense, defense of others, defense of property (never deadly force), recapture (fresh pursuit), shopkeeper, necessity (public is complete, private pays), discipline.

5. Damages. Nominal for battery, assault, and trespass to land; punitive damages for malice (Big Town, Katko, Fisher).

sections.title: 11. The Negligence Case and Unreasonable Risk
sections.html:
rule

The prima facie case for negligence

The plaintiff must prove all required:
(1) duty, an obligation to conform to a standard of conduct for the protection of others against unreasonable risks;
(2) breach, conduct that falls below that standard;
(3) cause in fact, the conduct was a but-for or substantial-factor cause of the harm;
(4) proximate cause, the harm is within the scope of the risk that made the conduct negligent; and
(5) damages, actual harm to person or property (nominal damages are not available).

  • Negligence is conduct, not a state of mind. It is the creation of an unreasonable risk of harm to others (R2d § 282). The plaintiff need not show the defendant knew of the risk, only that a reasonable person would have.
  • Duty and breach. The general duty is reasonable care toward foreseeable plaintiffs (§ 21 covers limits). The standard is the reasonable person under the same or similar circumstances (§ 12).
  • Unreasonable risk has two parts: (1) the risk must be foreseeable; and (2) a reasonable person would have taken a precaution against it, given its likelihood and severity and the burden of avoiding it.
main case

Lubitz v. Wells (Conn. Super. 1955) — foreseeability of harm

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.A

Facts: Mr. Wells left a golf club in his backyard. His son, J. Wells Jr., picked it up and swung it at a stone without warning Judith Lubitz, who was playing nearby, and hit her in the jaw. She sued the son for negligent swinging and the father for leaving the club where it could cause harm.

Held: Troland, J.: leaving a golf club in a yard is not negligent. It is not an inherently dangerous instrument, and the chance that a child would injure someone with it was not reasonably foreseeable. Demurrer as to the father sustained.

Why it matters: Without a foreseeable risk there is no negligence. Contrast a loaded gun or a dangerous chemical left where children play.

main case

Blyth v. Birmingham Waterworks Co. (Ex. 1856) — the classic definition

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.A

Facts: The waterworks company installed water mains and fire plugs that had worked properly for 25 years. During the severe frost of 1855, ice forced out a plug's stopper, and water flooded Blyth's house. The jury found for Blyth.

Held: Alderson, B.: negligence is "the omission to do something which a reasonable man, guided upon those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do." A reasonable company guards against ordinary frosts, not one of extraordinary severity. Reversed; judgment for the company.

Why it matters: This is the standard definition of negligence. Foreseeability is measured by ordinary experience at the time.

main case

Pipher v. Parsell (Del. 2007) — foreseeable conduct of a passenger

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.A

Facts: Parsell, 16, was driving two other 16-year-olds in a pickup truck at 55 mph, all three in the front seat. Passenger Biesel suddenly grabbed the wheel, and the truck veered toward the shoulder; Parsell regained control and did nothing. About 30 seconds later Biesel grabbed the wheel again; the truck left the road and hit a tree, injuring Pipher, the middle passenger. Parsell admitted at trial he could have told Biesel not to do it again, moved her, or made her get out. The trial judge ruled as a matter of law that Parsell had no duty to act after the first grab.

Held: Holland, J.: a driver owes passengers and the public a duty of reasonable care. When it is foreseeable that a passenger's conduct may interfere with safe driving, failing to prevent it may breach that duty. After the first grab, a reasonable jury could find the second foreseeable and Parsell's inaction a breach. Breach and proximate cause were jury questions. Reversed.

Why it matters: A Delaware Supreme Court case. Foreseeability can arise during the events, and whether the response was reasonable is usually for the jury.

rule

Weighing the risk: R2d §§ 291–293; R3d § 3

An act is negligent if its risk outweighs its utility. Factors weighed together:
(1) the foreseeable likelihood that the conduct will cause harm;
(2) the foreseeable severity of any harm; and
(3) the burden of precautions that would eliminate or reduce the risk, including the social value of the conduct.

main case

Chicago, B. & Q. R. Co. v. Krayenbuhl (Neb. 1902) — utility vs. danger

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.B

Facts: Children often played on the railroad's turntable, which was near a public path. Company rules required it to be padlocked when not in use, but the rule was often ignored. Four-year-old Krayenbuhl went there with other children, who found the turntable unlocked (or unlocked it), and his foot was caught and severed above the ankle. The jury found for him.

Held: A possessor who knows or has reason to know that young children will be attracted to a dangerous machine on its land must use reasonable care to protect them. Whether a precaution is required depends on balancing the machine's usefulness and the cost of the precaution against the danger. A lock costs little and would not impair the turntable's use. The judgment was reversed on other grounds (an error in the instructions).

Why it matters: This is risk-utility balancing before the Hand formula. It is also an ancestor of the attractive nuisance doctrine (§ 26).

main case

Davison v. Snohomish County (Wash. 1928) — burden of precautions

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.B

Facts: Coming off a county bridge onto a curved, elevated approach, Davison's car skidded, broke through the wooden guardrail, and fell. He claimed the rail was too weak to stop a car, the curve was improperly banked, and dirt on the road caused the skid. The jury found for Davison.

Held: Beals, J.: a county is not required to build guardrails strong enough to stop cars on all elevated roads. The cost would be prohibitive and would discourage building roads. The banking deviation was small in relation to the whole slope, and the county is not liable for an ordinary accumulation of dirt. Reversed.

Why it matters: The burden of the precaution, measured across all similar roads, can make a risk reasonable.

main case

United States v. Carroll Towing Co. (2d Cir. 1947) — the Hand formula

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.B

Facts: In January 1944, in crowded New York Harbor, the barge Anna C was moored with others at a pier. A tug crew employed by Carroll Towing negligently readjusted the mooring lines, and the barges broke loose. The Anna C drifted against a tanker, whose propeller holed her, and she sank with her cargo of government flour. Its bargee had been ashore for 21 hours, though barges were constantly being moved in the harbor. The trial court divided damages.

Held: Hand, J.: an owner's duty to guard against a barge breaking loose depends on three variables: (1) the probability that it will break away (P); (2) the gravity of the resulting injury (L); and (3) the burden of adequate precautions (B). Liability follows if B < P × L. Keeping a bargee aboard during the working hours of daylight, in a crowded wartime harbor, was a small burden compared with the risk. The owner's own negligence reduced its recovery. Affirmed.

Why it matters: This is the canonical risk-utility test. On an essay, put rough values on B, P, and L and compare them.

note

Using and criticizing the Hand formula

  • The formula compares the marginal (additional) precaution with the marginal reduction in risk.
  • Values are often unquantifiable, and juries rarely do the arithmetic. Courts use it as a way to organize the argument.
  • Critics say it values harm by market measures, such as lost earnings, which can undervalue harm to lower-income people, and that it treats safety as just another cost.

sections.title: 12. The Reasonable Person
sections.html:
rule

The standard: R2d § 283; R3d § 3

The standard of conduct is that of a reasonable person of ordinary prudence under the same or similar circumstances. It is objective: the actor's own good faith or best judgment does not count (Vaughan v. Menlove).

Characteristic

Rule

Case

Lack of judgment or intelligence

No allowance; the objective standard applies

Vaughan v. Menlove

Knowledge

Charged with what a reasonable person knows, including common facts and knowledge from reasonable inspection; superior knowledge counts

Delair v. McAdoo

Custom

Evidence of due care, not conclusive

Trimarco v. Klein

Emergency

A reasonable person in that emergency, if not of the actor's making

Cordas v. Peerless

Physical disability

A reasonable person with that disability

Roberts v. Louisiana

Children

A child of like age, intelligence, and experience, except in adult activities

Robinson v. Lindsay

Mental illness

No allowance, except sudden mental incapacity without warning

Breunig

Intoxication

Held to the standard of a sober person

(no case; R2d § 283C cmt. d)

main case

Vaughan v. Menlove (C.P. 1837) — objective standard

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.B

Facts: Menlove built a hayrick near the edge of his land, beside Vaughan's cottages. He was warned several times that it was likely to catch fire. He said his stock was insured and he "would chance it," though he cut a chimney through it as a precaution. The hay ignited spontaneously, and the fire destroyed Vaughan's cottages. Menlove argued he should be liable only if he failed to act honestly and to the best of his own judgment.

Held: Tindal, C.J.: the standard is objective: whether the defendant used the caution a man of ordinary prudence would use. A standard based on each individual's judgment would be "as variable as the length of the foot of each individual." The verdict for Vaughan stood.

Why it matters: This is the origin of the objective standard. Low intelligence is no excuse.

main case

Delair v. McAdoo (Pa. 1936) — knowledge charged to everyone

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: McAdoo tried to pass Delair's car when his left rear tire blew out, and his car crashed into Delair's. Witnesses said the tire was worn through to the fabric. McAdoo said he did not know the tires were worn. The jury found for Delair.

Held: Kephart, C.J.: every adult is charged with knowledge of facts common to the community, such as gravity, fire, and the danger of worn tires. The owner or operator of a car is charged with knowledge of its condition that a reasonable inspection would reveal, and the wear here was visible. Affirmed.

Why it matters: A defendant cannot plead ignorance of what everyone knows. Inspection duties arise from the activity.

main case

Trimarco v. Klein (N.Y. 1982) — custom as evidence

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: Trimarco, a tenant in Klein's building, was badly cut when he fell through the glass door of his bathtub enclosure. The door was ordinary thin glass, though it looked like tempered glass. His expert testified that by the 1950s it had become the common practice of landlords to use shatterproof glass in such enclosures. The jury found for Trimarco, but the Appellate Division reversed, holding the landlord had no duty to replace the glass without notice of the danger.

Held: Fuchsberg, J.: evidence of custom and usage by others in the same business is admissible to show what is reasonable, but it is not conclusive. Quoting Holmes: "What usually is done may be evidence of what ought to be done, but what ought to be done is fixed by a standard of reasonable prudence, whether it usually is complied with or not." The custom evidence was properly admitted. A new trial was ordered because of other erroneously admitted evidence.

Why it matters: Custom is a sword (deviation is evidence of negligence) and a shield (compliance is evidence of care), but never conclusive. The T.J. Hooper (2d Cir. 1932, Hand, J.) holds that a whole industry can lag behind reasonable care.

main case

Cordas v. Peerless Transportation Co. (N.Y. City Ct. 1941) — sudden emergency

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: A man who had just committed a robbery, chased by a crowd shouting "Stop thief," jumped into a Peerless cab, pointed a gun at the driver, and ordered him to drive. The driver started off, then threw the car out of gear, braked, and jumped out. The cab, still moving, mounted the sidewalk and hit Mrs. Cordas and her two children.

Held: Carlin, J.: a person faced with a sudden emergency not of his own making is not held to the judgment he would use with time to reflect. He is judged by what a reasonable person would do in that emergency. The driver was not negligent; the law does not require heroism. Complaint dismissed.

Why it matters: The emergency is a circumstance, not a separate standard. It does not help someone whose own negligence created the emergency.

main case

Roberts v. State of Louisiana (La. App. 1981) — physical disability

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: Burson, a blind man, ran a snack bar in a state office building. He left the counter to go to the restroom without his cane, relying on his familiarity with the area and his "facial sense" of nearby obstacles, and bumped into Roberts, who fell and hurt his hip. Roberts sued the state as Burson's employer and for negligent supervision. His only evidence of Burson's negligence was an expert who had never examined Burson. The trial court dismissed.

Held: Laborde, J.: a person with a physical disability must take the precautions that a reasonable person with the same disability would take. Burson's evidence showed his method of moving through familiar areas was reasonable, and Roberts did not prove otherwise. Affirmed.

Why it matters: The disability is part of the circumstances, so the standard is a reasonable blind person, not a reasonable sighted one.

main case

Robinson v. Lindsay (Wash. 1979) — children in adult activities

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: Billy Anderson, 13, was driving a snowmobile when an accident injured Kelly Robinson, 11, who lost full use of her thumb. The jury was instructed to judge Billy by the standard of a reasonable child of his age and found for him. The trial judge then granted a new trial, ruling that an adult standard should have applied.

Held: Utter, C.J.: children are generally held to the standard of a reasonable child of like age, intelligence, and experience. But a child engaged in an inherently dangerous activity normally pursued only by adults, such as operating a powerful motorized vehicle, is held to the adult standard. Snowmobiles qualify. The new trial was properly ordered. Affirmed.

Why it matters: This is the adult-activity exception. Some states hold that children under a set age, often 5 or 7, are incapable of negligence (tender-years rule).

main case

Breunig v. American Family Ins. Co. (Wis. 1970) — sudden mental illness

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: Erma Veith, insured by American Family, was driving when she believed God was taking control of her car. Seeing a truck ahead, she stepped on the gas so the car would become airborne, believing she could fly like Batman. Her car crossed the center line and hit Breunig's truck. A psychiatrist testified she had a sudden delusion; there was also evidence she had had similar visions before. The jury found her negligent.

Held: Hallows, C.J.: insanity is generally no defense to negligence, for policy reasons weighed together: (1) between two innocent people, the one who caused the loss should bear it; (2) liability gives those interested in an insane person's estate a reason to restrain him; and (3) it prevents false claims of insanity. But a sudden mental incapacity that strikes without warning, like a heart attack or epileptic seizure, is an exception. Because the jury could find Veith had forewarning of her delusions, the verdict for Breunig was affirmed.

Why it matters: The general rule rests on policies weighed together:
(1) between two innocent people, the one who caused the loss should bear it;
(2) it encourages those responsible for the mentally ill to control them; and
(3) it prevents false claims of insanity. Compare Cohen v. Petty (§ 1).

note

Bias lens: whose "reasonable"?

  • The "reasonable man" became the "reasonable person." Critics argue the standard can still build in the perspective of the people who historically served as jurors and judges.
  • Roberts takes disability into account, but mental illness gets no allowance (Breunig). Consider whether that distinction is principled.
  • Some scholars argue for a "reasonable woman" standard in harassment contexts, or for considering the plaintiff's community when judging what is offensive or reasonable.

sections.title: 13. Professionals and Informed Consent
sections.html:
rule

The professional standard

A professional must use all required:
(1) the knowledge and skill ordinarily possessed by members of the profession in good standing (in the same specialty and, under older rules, the same or a similar locality);
(2) reasonable care and diligence in applying that knowledge and skill; and
(3) his best judgment.

Proof: the standard and its breach must be shown by expert testimony unless the negligence is obvious to a layperson, such as leaving a sponge in the patient or operating on the wrong limb (Boyce).

note

Restatement (Third): duties of medical providers

R3d Medical Malpractice §§ 2–3 (approved 2022): a patient-care relationship arises when a provider manifests an intent to care for a patient and any one suffices
(1) begins care without the patient's objection;
(2) the patient reasonably believes the provider has undertaken care; or
(3) the patient reasonably relies on the provider.

Duties within the relationship (all owed):
(1) to exercise reasonable care;
(2) to comply with the requirements of informed consent;
(3) to use reasonable care to protect confidential patient information; and
(4) not to end the relationship without giving the patient a reasonable opportunity to find other care.

  • Professional custom sets the standard. Unlike ordinary custom (Trimarco), what the profession does is the measure of care, not just evidence of it.
  • Schools of thought: a doctor who follows a method accepted by a respectable minority of the profession is not negligent.
  • Error in judgment: a professional is not liable for an honest error in an area where reasonable professionals disagree or the law is unsettled (Hodges).
  • Specialists are held to the standard of a reasonable specialist in that field, usually national (Morrison).
main case

Heath v. Swift Wings, Inc. (N.C. App. 1979) — objective professional standard

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: A small plane crashed shortly after takeoff, killing the pilot and his passengers. In the passengers' estates' suit against the pilot's estate, the jury was instructed that negligence meant failing to use the care that "an ordinarily prudent pilot having the same training and experience as" this pilot would use. The jury found the pilot not negligent.

Held: Morris, C.J.: the instruction was wrong. A professional's standard is objective: the care of a reasonably prudent pilot with the knowledge and skill the profession requires. Tying the standard to the defendant's own training and experience would create a different standard for every defendant. New trial ordered.

Why it matters: Even professionals are judged objectively. "Best judgment" is required, but it is not enough by itself.

main case

Hodges v. Carter (N.C. 1954) — lawyer's error in judgment

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: Hodges's drugstore and its contents burned, and his four fire insurers refused to pay. His lawyers, Topping and Carter, sued and served process on the foreign insurers by mail through the state Commissioner of Insurance, the method in standard use for more than 20 years. The North Carolina Supreme Court then held that method invalid, and the limitations period had run. Hodges sued the lawyers for negligence, including their failure to obtain new summonses in time. The trial court entered a nonsuit.

Held: Barnhill, C.J.: a lawyer is liable if the client's loss results from (1) a lack of the knowledge and skill ordinarily possessed by lawyers similarly situated, (2) a failure to use reasonable care and diligence, or (3) a failure to use his best judgment. A lawyer who acts in good faith and follows the settled practice of the bar is not liable for a mistake on a point of law later decided against him. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Lawyers are not guarantors of results. They are liable for lacking ordinary skill, for failing to use reasonable care, or for not using their best judgment.

main case

Boyce v. Brown (Ariz. 1938) — expert testimony required

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: In 1927, Dr. Brown set Mrs. Boyce's fractured ankle by surgically inserting a metal screw. In 1934 she returned with a swollen, painful ankle; he taped it and filed down her arch support but took no X-ray. In 1936, Dr. Kent X-rayed the ankle, found the bone around the screw had deteriorated, and removed the screw; she recovered. At trial, Dr. Kent testified about what he did in 1936 but not about the standard of care in 1934. The trial court directed a verdict for Dr. Brown.

Held: Lockwood, J.: medical negligence must be proved by expert testimony that the doctor departed from the accepted standard of practice, unless the negligence is so grossly apparent that a layperson would have no difficulty recognizing it. A different method is not negligence, and failing to take an X-ray is not obvious negligence. Affirmed.

Why it matters: The plaintiff's expert must address the standard and the breach, not just what he would have done.

main case

Morrison v. MacNamara (D.C. 1979) — national standard of care

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: MacNamara, a nationally accredited medical laboratory in Washington, D.C., performed a urethral smear test for trichomonas on Morrison while he stood. He fainted and was seriously injured in the fall. The court excluded his expert's testimony that the national standard was to perform the test with the patient sitting or lying down, but admitted local doctors' testimony that in D.C. it was done standing. The jury found for the laboratory.

Held: Newman, C.J.: the standard of care for board-certified physicians, hospitals, medical laboratories, and other health care providers is national. The locality rule was premised on disparities between urban and rural medicine that national certification has removed, and it can shield substandard local practice. The expert's testimony should have been admitted. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: The locality rule is giving way to a national standard, at least for specialists and accredited facilities. Some states use a "same or similar locality" rule.

rule

Informed consent: Scott v. Bradford

The plaintiff must prove all required:
(1) the physician failed to disclose a material risk of, or alternative to, the treatment;
(2) had the risk been disclosed, the plaintiff would have declined the treatment (causation); and
(3) the undisclosed risk materialized and injured the plaintiff.

Exceptions any one suffices:
(1) emergency;
(2) the risk was known to the patient or is common knowledge;
(3) disclosure would seriously harm the patient (therapeutic privilege); or
(4) the patient waived disclosure.

Question

Patient-oriented view (Scott; Canterbury v. Spence)

Physician-oriented view (traditional)

What must be disclosed?

What a reasonable patient would find material to the decision

What a reasonable physician would disclose (professional custom)

Expert testimony?

Not needed on what to disclose

Needed to prove the custom

Causation

Scott: subjective (would this patient have refused?). Canterbury and most courts: objective (would a reasonable patient have refused?)

Usually objective

main case

Scott v. Bradford (Okla. 1979) — informed consent

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: Dr. Bradford performed a hysterectomy on Mrs. Scott to remove fibroid tumors. He did not tell her of the risks or of alternatives to surgery. After the operation she suffered incontinence and needed several corrective operations. She testified she would have refused the surgery had she been told. The jury found for the doctor.

Held: Doolin, J.: a doctor must disclose the material risks of, and alternatives to, a proposed treatment. To recover, the patient must prove (1) the doctor failed to inform her of a material risk; (2) had she been informed, she would not have consented (judged subjectively, by her own testimony); and (3) the undisclosed risk occurred and injured her. The jury was properly instructed and simply did not believe she would have refused. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Informed consent protects patient autonomy, and it is a negligence claim, not battery. Oklahoma's subjective causation test is the minority view.

main case

Moore v. Regents of the University of California (Cal. 1990) — disclosure of the physician's interests

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C

Facts: Moore was treated for hairy-cell leukemia at UCLA Medical Center by Dr. Golde. Golde learned that Moore's cells had unusual commercial value. Without telling him, Golde removed his spleen and, over seven years, took blood and other samples, developing a patented cell line with potential value in the billions. Moore sued for conversion, breach of fiduciary duty, and lack of informed consent. The trial court dismissed.

Held: Panelli, J.: a physician must disclose personal interests unrelated to the patient's health, whether research or economic, that may affect his medical judgment. Failing to disclose states a claim for breach of fiduciary duty or lack of informed consent. But the court refused to recognize a conversion claim for the cells, because extending conversion would chill medical research. Remanded.

Why it matters: The disclosure duty extends to conflicts of interest. Note the bias and consent issues: compare the Henrietta Lacks cell line.

sections.title: 14. Judge and Jury; Negligence Per Se
Judge and jury
sections.html:
• The judge decides duty and whether the evidence is sufficient. The jury applies the standard of care to the facts, unless reasonable people could not disagree, in which case the judge decides as a matter of law.
  • Judges sometimes try to fix specific standards of conduct as rules of law, as in Holmes's "stop, look, and get out" rule for railroad crossings (Goodman, 1927). Cardozo limited that approach in Pokora.
main case

Pokora v. Wabash Ry. Co. (U.S. 1934) — standards for the jury

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.D

Facts: Pokora drove his truck to a four-track railroad crossing. Boxcars on the first track blocked his view to the north. He stopped, looked, and listened, heard nothing, and drove slowly forward without getting out to look. On the main track he was hit by a train from the north. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad on contributory negligence, citing Holmes's rule in Baltimore & Ohio R.R. v. Goodman (1927) that a driver who cannot see must get out and look.

Held: Cardozo, J.: failing to get out of the vehicle to reconnoiter was not contributory negligence as a matter of law. Getting out may be futile, or more dangerous than not, since the train may arrive while the driver walks back. Standards of prudent conduct are ordinarily for the jury, and Goodman's rule must be confined. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: Cardozo limited Goodman. Judges should rarely fix standards of conduct, which vary with the circumstances.

rule

Negligence per se: R2d §§ 286, 288A; R3d § 14

An unexcused violation of a statute is negligence when all required:
(1) the statute prescribes specific conduct for the safety of others;
(2) the defendant violated it without excuse;
(3) the plaintiff is within the class of persons the statute was designed to protect;
(4) the harm is of the type the statute was designed to prevent; and
(5) the violation caused the harm (cause in fact and proximate cause).

Effect of an unexcused violation

Approach

Case

Negligence as a matter of law (per se); the jury decides only causation and damages

Majority

Martin v. Herzog; Osborne

A rebuttable presumption of negligence; the defendant may prove an excuse

Many states, and R2d § 288A in practice

Zeni v. Anderson

Evidence of negligence that the jury may weigh

Minority (e.g., ordinances, traffic rules in some states)

Ney v. Yellow Cab (prima facie evidence)

Excuses, R2d § 288A(2) any one suffices:
(a) the violation is reasonable because of the actor's incapacity;
(b) he neither knows nor should know of the occasion for compliance;
(c) he is unable after reasonable diligence or care to comply;
(d) he is confronted by an emergency not due to his own misconduct; or
(e) compliance would involve a greater risk of harm to the actor or to others.

rule

The plaintiff's own violations: R3d Misc. Prov., Apportionment §§ 4 A–4 B (approved 2022)

§ 4 A (wrongful acts doctrine): a person injured by tortious conduct is not barred from recovery merely because she was engaged in an illegal, tortious, or otherwise wrongful act at the time.

§ 4 B(a): an injured victim is negligent if, without excuse, she violates a criminal statute or other safety regulation designed to protect against the type of accident her conduct caused, and she is within the class the statute protects. § 4 B(b): if that negligence is a factual cause of her harm, it reduces her recovery under comparative responsibility; otherwise it has no effect. This is negligence per se applied to the plaintiff, as in Martin v. Herzog and Zeni v. Anderson.

main case

Osborne v. McMasters (Minn. 1889) — statute fixes the duty

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: A clerk in McMasters's drugstore, acting in the course of his employment, sold a deadly poison to Osborne's decedent without labeling it "poison," as a criminal statute required. The decedent took it by mistake and died.

Held: Mitchell, J.: where a statute imposes a specific duty for the protection of others, one who neglects that duty is liable to those it was meant to protect, for the kind of injury it was meant to prevent and that the violation proximately caused. Negligence is the breach of a legal duty, whether the duty comes from common law or statute. The employer is liable for the clerk's breach. Affirmed.

Why it matters: This is the classic statement of negligence per se and its class-of-persons and type-of-harm limits.

main case

Stachniewicz v. Mar-Cam Corp. (Or. 1971) — class of persons and type of harm

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: A fight broke out in Mar-Cam's bar between a group in a booth, some visibly intoxicated, and Stachniewicz's party at a nearby table, after one of the group had been refused a dance. The bartender had received complaints about the group. Stachniewicz was later found unconscious outside the door with retrograde amnesia. He relied on Oregon Liquor Control Commission regulations barring service to visibly intoxicated persons and barring licensees from permitting loud, noisy, disorderly, or boisterous conduct on the premises. The trial court refused to treat the violations as negligence per se, and the jury found for the bar.

Held: Holman, J.: violation of a statute or regulation is negligence as a matter of law when the injured person is in the class protected and the harm is the kind the rule was meant to prevent. The regulation against permitting disorderly conduct bears directly on the start of fights, so it was meant to protect patrons from this kind of injury, and the jury could infer his injuries came from the fight. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: Courts often infer the legislature's purpose from the statute's text when legislative history is thin, which gives them latitude.

main case

Ney v. Yellow Cab Co. (Ill. 1954) — key-in-the-ignition statute

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: A Yellow Cab driver left his cab unattended and unlocked with the key in the ignition, in violation of an Illinois Uniform Traffic Act section. A thief stole it and, while driving it, collided with Ney's car. The jury found for Ney, and the appellate court affirmed. Yellow Cab argued the statute was only a traffic regulation, not a safety measure.

Held: Maxwell, J.: the statute was meant to protect public safety, including against the dangers of stolen cars driven carelessly, so its violation is prima facie evidence of negligence. Whether the thief's intervening crime cut off proximate cause was a fact question for the jury, which resolved it for Ney. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Purpose decides class and harm. Courts split on key-in-ignition cases, and many find the thief's act superseding (§ 20).

Dissent (Hershey, J.): leaving a key in the ignition is a minor cause of theft, the statute was not aimed at this harm, and the thief's act should be the proximate cause.

main case

Perry v. S.N. (Tex. 1998) — when courts decline negligence per se

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: Two children attended a day-care center run by the Kellers, where Daniel Keller allegedly abused them physically and sexually. The parents sued the Kellers and three of their friends, Perry, White, and Quintero, who allegedly saw the abuse and did not report it, as the Texas Family Code required of anyone who believes a child is being abused. The trial court granted summary judgment for the friends; the court of appeals reversed on negligence per se.

Held: Phillips, C.J.: the children were in the protected class and suffered the type of harm the statute addressed, but that is not enough. Weighing factors against adopting the statute as a tort standard weighed together: (1) there is no common-law duty to report, so the statute would be the only source of the duty; (2) the statute does not clearly define when its duty arises; (3) liability would be imposed without regard to fault; (4) the injury results only indirectly from the violation, through the abuser's crime; and (5) the liability would be ruinous and out of proportion to the conduct, and would fall on a broad class of people. Violation of the reporting statute is not negligence per se. Reversed.

Why it matters: Adopting a statute as the standard of care is a judicial choice. It is not automatic.

main case

Martin v. Herzog (N.Y. 1920) — unexcused violation is negligence itself

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: Martin was driving a buggy at night without lights, in violation of a statute, when it collided with Herzog's car, which was coming around a curve without keeping to the right. Martin was killed. The trial judge instructed that driving without lights was not negligence in itself but only evidence of negligence. The jury found for Martin's estate; the Appellate Division reversed.

Held: Cardozo, J.: the unexcused omission of a statutory safeguard is negligence in itself, not just evidence of it. Jurors have no power to relax a duty the statute imposes for the protection of other travelers. But the violation must also be a cause of the accident. Evidence that a car hit an unlighted buggy at night supports an inference that the lack of lights contributed. Affirmed (new trial).

Why it matters: Negligence per se determines breach, but causation is still required. A violation that did not contribute to the harm does not matter.

main case

Zeni v. Anderson (Mich. 1976) — rebuttable presumption and excuse

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: On a snowy winter morning, Zeni was walking to work. Rather than use the snow-covered sidewalk, she walked on a well-used path in the street, with her back to traffic, in violation of a statute requiring pedestrians to use sidewalks or face traffic. Anderson's car, possibly too close to the curb, hit her. The jury found for Zeni; the court of appeals reversed on the ground that her violation was negligence per se.

Held: Williams, J.: violation of a statute creates a rebuttable presumption of negligence, which the violator may overcome by showing an adequate excuse. Rigid per se treatment would ignore reasonable justifications, like an impassable sidewalk. The issue was properly left to the jury. Reversed; verdict for Zeni reinstated.

Why it matters: This is the modern middle position, and it reflects R2d § 288A excuses.

trap

Traps to avoid

  • Compliance with a statute is evidence of care, but not conclusive. The reasonable person may have to do more (R2d § 288C).
  • Licensing statutes usually do not support negligence per se. Practicing without a license does not prove the treatment was negligent (Brown v. Shyne, N.Y. 1926).
  • Check the purpose. A statute aimed at a different harm (e.g., a Sunday-closing law) does not make a violator liable for an unrelated accident.

sections.title: 15. Circumstantial Evidence and Notice
