cases.title: Stachniewicz v. Mar-Cam Corp. (Or. 1971) — class of persons and type of harm
cases.html:
main case

Stachniewicz v. Mar-Cam Corp. (Or. 1971) — class of persons and type of harm

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: A fight broke out in Mar-Cam's bar between a group in a booth, some visibly intoxicated, and Stachniewicz's party at a nearby table, after one of the group had been refused a dance. The bartender had received complaints about the group. Stachniewicz was later found unconscious outside the door with retrograde amnesia. He relied on Oregon Liquor Control Commission regulations barring service to visibly intoxicated persons and barring licensees from permitting loud, noisy, disorderly, or boisterous conduct on the premises. The trial court refused to treat the violations as negligence per se, and the jury found for the bar.

Held: Holman, J.: violation of a statute or regulation is negligence as a matter of law when the injured person is in the class protected and the harm is the kind the rule was meant to prevent. The regulation against permitting disorderly conduct bears directly on the start of fights, so it was meant to protect patrons from this kind of injury, and the jury could infer his injuries came from the fight. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: Courts often infer the legislature's purpose from the statute's text when legislative history is thin, which gives them latitude.

cases.name: Ney v. Yellow Cab Co.
cases.title: Ney v. Yellow Cab Co. (Ill. 1954) — key-in-the-ignition statute
cases.html:
main case

Ney v. Yellow Cab Co. (Ill. 1954) — key-in-the-ignition statute

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: A Yellow Cab driver left his cab unattended and unlocked with the key in the ignition, in violation of an Illinois Uniform Traffic Act section. A thief stole it and, while driving it, collided with Ney's car. The jury found for Ney, and the appellate court affirmed. Yellow Cab argued the statute was only a traffic regulation, not a safety measure.

Held: Maxwell, J.: the statute was meant to protect public safety, including against the dangers of stolen cars driven carelessly, so its violation is prima facie evidence of negligence. Whether the thief's intervening crime cut off proximate cause was a fact question for the jury, which resolved it for Ney. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Purpose decides class and harm. Courts split on key-in-ignition cases, and many find the thief's act superseding (§ 20).

Dissent (Hershey, J.): leaving a key in the ignition is a minor cause of theft, the statute was not aimed at this harm, and the thief's act should be the proximate cause.

cases.name: Perry v. S.N.
cases.title: Perry v. S.N. (Tex. 1998) — when courts decline negligence per se
cases.html:
main case

Perry v. S.N. (Tex. 1998) — when courts decline negligence per se

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: Two children attended a day-care center run by the Kellers, where Daniel Keller allegedly abused them physically and sexually. The parents sued the Kellers and three of their friends, Perry, White, and Quintero, who allegedly saw the abuse and did not report it, as the Texas Family Code required of anyone who believes a child is being abused. The trial court granted summary judgment for the friends; the court of appeals reversed on negligence per se.

Held: Phillips, C.J.: the children were in the protected class and suffered the type of harm the statute addressed, but that is not enough. Weighing factors against adopting the statute as a tort standard weighed together: (1) there is no common-law duty to report, so the statute would be the only source of the duty; (2) the statute does not clearly define when its duty arises; (3) liability would be imposed without regard to fault; (4) the injury results only indirectly from the violation, through the abuser's crime; and (5) the liability would be ruinous and out of proportion to the conduct, and would fall on a broad class of people. Violation of the reporting statute is not negligence per se. Reversed.

Why it matters: Adopting a statute as the standard of care is a judicial choice. It is not automatic.

cases.name: Martin v. Herzog
cases.title: Martin v. Herzog (N.Y. 1920) — unexcused violation is negligence itself
cases.html:
main case

Martin v. Herzog (N.Y. 1920) — unexcused violation is negligence itself

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: Martin was driving a buggy at night without lights, in violation of a statute, when it collided with Herzog's car, which was coming around a curve without keeping to the right. Martin was killed. The trial judge instructed that driving without lights was not negligence in itself but only evidence of negligence. The jury found for Martin's estate; the Appellate Division reversed.

Held: Cardozo, J.: the unexcused omission of a statutory safeguard is negligence in itself, not just evidence of it. Jurors have no power to relax a duty the statute imposes for the protection of other travelers. But the violation must also be a cause of the accident. Evidence that a car hit an unlighted buggy at night supports an inference that the lack of lights contributed. Affirmed (new trial).

Why it matters: Negligence per se determines breach, but causation is still required. A violation that did not contribute to the harm does not matter.

cases.name: Zeni v. Anderson
cases.title: Zeni v. Anderson (Mich. 1976) — rebuttable presumption and excuse
cases.html:
main case

Zeni v. Anderson (Mich. 1976) — rebuttable presumption and excuse

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E

Facts: On a snowy winter morning, Zeni was walking to work. Rather than use the snow-covered sidewalk, she walked on a well-used path in the street, with her back to traffic, in violation of a statute requiring pedestrians to use sidewalks or face traffic. Anderson's car, possibly too close to the curb, hit her. The jury found for Zeni; the court of appeals reversed on the ground that her violation was negligence per se.

Held: Williams, J.: violation of a statute creates a rebuttable presumption of negligence, which the violator may overcome by showing an adequate excuse. Rigid per se treatment would ignore reasonable justifications, like an impassable sidewalk. The issue was properly left to the jury. Reversed; verdict for Zeni reinstated.

Why it matters: This is the modern middle position, and it reflects R2d § 288A excuses.

cases.name: Goddard v. Boston & Maine R.R. Co.
cases.title: Goddard v. Boston & Maine R.R. Co. (Mass. 1901) — no evidence of notice
cases.html:
main case

Goddard v. Boston & Maine R.R. Co. (Mass. 1901) — no evidence of notice

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F

Facts: Goddard got off a train and walked the length of a car along the platform, where many other passengers had just alighted. He slipped on a banana skin and fell. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad.

Held: Holmes, C.J.: the banana skin could have been dropped by one of the departing passengers within a minute before the fall. Without evidence it had been there long enough for the railroad to discover it, there was no negligence. Exceptions overruled.

Why it matters: This is the first of the banana-peel cases: no evidence of time means no constructive notice.

cases.name: Anjou v. Boston Elevated Railway Co.
cases.title: Anjou v. Boston Elevated Railway Co. (Mass. 1911) — circumstantial evidence of time
cases.html:
main case

Anjou v. Boston Elevated Railway Co. (Mass. 1911) — circumstantial evidence of time

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F

Facts: Anjou got off a train at the Dudley Street terminal, waited for the crowd to clear, and followed a uniformed railway employee along a narrow platform toward a stairway he pointed out. She slipped on a banana peel and was hurt. Witnesses described the peel as dry, gritty, black, flattened, and trampled over. The trial court directed a verdict for the railway.

Held: Rugg, J.: the railway had a duty to keep its platform reasonably safe, including by watching for and removing debris. From the peel's condition, the jury could infer it had been on the platform long enough to be discovered and removed. Exceptions sustained; judgment for Anjou under the terms of the report.

Why it matters: The condition of the object can supply the evidence of time that Goddard lacked.

cases.name: Joye v. Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Co.
cases.title: Joye v. Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Co. (4th Cir. 1968) — speculation is not enough
cases.html:
main case

Joye v. Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Co. (4th Cir. 1968) — speculation is not enough

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F

Facts: Joye slipped on a banana in an A&P supermarket aisle. The banana was dark brown, sticky at the edges, and had dirt and sand on it, and the floor was dirty. The aisle may not have been swept for 35 minutes. No one knew how long the banana had been there or how it got there. The jury awarded Joye $10,000.

Held: Craven, J.: without evidence of how long the hazard existed, there is no constructive notice. On this record a "jury could not tell whether the banana had been on A&P's floor for thirty seconds or three days." Reversed.

Why it matters: A banana that browns on its own does not show how long it has been on the floor. Compare Anjou.

cases.name: Ortega v. Kmart Corp.
cases.title: Ortega v. Kmart Corp. (Cal. 2001) — inference from failure to inspect
cases.html:
main case

Ortega v. Kmart Corp. (Cal. 2001) — inference from failure to inspect

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F

Facts: Ortega slipped on a puddle of milk in a Kmart and seriously injured his knee. He could not prove how long the milk had been there, but he showed Kmart had not inspected the area for 15 to 30 minutes, and perhaps as long as two hours. The jury awarded $47,000.

Held: Chin, J.: a store owner must make reasonable inspections of areas customers use. The plaintiff may prove constructive notice by circumstantial evidence that the condition existed long enough for a reasonably prudent owner to discover and correct it, including evidence that the owner failed to inspect within a reasonable time. He need not prove exactly how long the hazard was there. Affirmed.

Why it matters: The focus shifts from how long the hazard was there to how reasonable the inspection program was.

cases.name: Jasko v. F.W. Woolworth Co.
cases.title: Jasko v. F.W. Woolworth Co. (Colo. 1972) — mode of operation
cases.html:
main case

Jasko v. F.W. Woolworth Co. (Colo. 1972) — mode of operation

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F

Facts: Jasko slipped on a slice of pizza on the terrazzo floor near Woolworth's "Pizza Hoagie Counter." Woolworth sold pizza by the slice on waxed paper to customers who often ate standing up, and it had employees clean the floor constantly. Jasko offered no evidence of how long the slice had been there. The trial court ruled for Woolworth.

Held: Groves, J.: when a proprietor's method of operation makes dangerous conditions continuous or easily foreseeable, the plaintiff need not prove notice of the particular condition. The notice rule assumes dangers are unusual, and that assumption fails when the danger comes from the way the store chooses to operate. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: The mode-of-operation rule reaches self-service and food-on-the-floor settings, where the danger comes from how the store chooses to operate.

cases.name: H.E. Butt Grocery Co. v. Resendez
cases.title: H.E. Butt Grocery Co. v. Resendez (Tex. 1999) — limits of mode of operation
cases.html:
main case

H.E. Butt Grocery Co. v. Resendez (Tex. 1999) — limits of mode of operation

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F

Facts: H-E-B displayed grapes in a bowl for customers to sample. The bowl sat on ice about five inches below the tabletop, and a three-inch rail ran around the table's edge. The floor was non-skid, mats surrounded the display, and warning cones stood nearby. Resendez slipped near the display. The jury found for her, and the court of appeals affirmed.

Held: Per curiam: merely displaying produce for customer sampling, without more, does not create an unreasonable risk of harm. Resendez had to prove all required (1) actual or constructive knowledge of a condition; (2) that the condition posed an unreasonable risk; (3) the store's failure to use reasonable care to reduce it; and (4) causation. She failed on (2). Unlike the slanted display without mats in Corbin v. Safeway (Tex. 1983), H-E-B's display had safeguards. Reversed; judgment for H-E-B.

Why it matters: Texas rejects mode-of-operation liability. Distinguish Jasko by the store's precautions and the jurisdiction's rule.

cases.name: Byrne v. Boadle
cases.title: Byrne v. Boadle (Ex. 1863) — the thing speaks for itself
cases.html:
main case

Byrne v. Boadle (Ex. 1863) — the thing speaks for itself

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G

Facts: Byrne was walking on a public street past Boadle's flour shop when a barrel of flour fell from an upper window and hit him. He had no evidence of why it fell. The trial judge nonsuited him for lack of evidence of negligence.

Held: Pollock, C.B.: "A barrel could not roll out of a warehouse without some negligence." The fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of negligence, and the plaintiff is not bound to show it could not have happened without negligence. If there are facts consistent with due care, the defendant, who controls the barrel and knows what happened, must prove them. Rule absolute to enter the verdict for Byrne.

Why it matters: This is the origin of res ipsa: an inference from the event itself, when the defendant has better access to the evidence.

cases.name: McDougald v. Perry
cases.title: McDougald v. Perry (Fla. 1998) — res ipsa from common experience: the flying spare tire
cases.html:
main case

McDougald v. Perry (Fla. 1998) — res ipsa from common experience: the flying spare tire

Source: Canvas reading (10/6), from the opinion text in the course folder.

Facts: On July 26, 1990, McDougald was driving his Jeep Wagoneer behind a tractor-trailer that Perry was driving for his employer, C & S Chemicals, on U.S. Highway 60 in Bartow, Florida. As the truck crossed railroad tracks, its 130-pound spare tire came out of its cradle under the trailer and fell to the road. The trailer's rear wheels ran over it, and it bounced up and smashed McDougald's windshield. The spare sat in an angled cradle, held by its own weight and by a four-to-six-foot chain that Perry believed was the original chain from 1969. The chain had originally been fastened with a latch but was now held by a nut and bolt. Perry had done a pre-trip inspection but did not check every link. Afterward the chain was dragging, and he thought a link had stretched and slipped off the bolt. The chain was not preserved. The jury, instructed on res ipsa loquitur, found for McDougald. The district court of appeal reversed, holding that McDougald had not proved the accident would not ordinarily occur without negligence.

Held: Wells, J.: res ipsa is a rule of evidence that permits, but does not compel, an inference of negligence. The plaintiff must show (1) the instrumentality was in the defendant's exclusive control and (2) the accident would not, in the ordinary course of events, have occurred without negligence by the one in control. Common experience shows that a spare tire carried on a truck, like a wheel on its axle, stays with the truck unless someone fails to use reasonable care: "no one expects the air to be filled with flying hubcaps." The plaintiff need not eliminate every other possible cause; it is enough that negligence is more likely than not. And direct proof was unavailable, because the chain and fastener were in the defendants' possession and were not preserved. The doctrine still applies only in "rare instances." Decision quashed; the jury's verdict on liability reinstated.

Why it matters: Common knowledge can supply the first element without expert testimony (R2d § 328D cmts. c–d). Contrast events that often happen without negligence, like a tire blowout or a fall down stairs. The defendant's control of the evidence strengthens the inference.

Concurrence (Anstead, J.): the result follows directly from Byrne v. Boadle (§ 16): "The common law tradition is alive and well."

cases.name: Larson v. St. Francis Hotel
cases.title: Larson v. St. Francis Hotel (Cal. App. 1948) — no exclusive control
cases.html:
main case

Larson v. St. Francis Hotel (Cal. App. 1948) — no exclusive control

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G

Facts: On August 14, 1945, V-J Day, crowds were celebrating in San Francisco. Just after Larson stepped out from under the St. Francis Hotel's marquee onto the sidewalk, a heavy overstuffed armchair fell from an upper window and knocked her unconscious. No one saw where it came from. The trial court granted a nonsuit.

Held: Bray, J.: res ipsa loquitur applies only if the instrumentality was under the defendant's exclusive control and management. Hotel guests, who rent rooms and use the furniture, have partial control. The likeliest explanation was that a celebrating guest threw the chair, which the hotel could not prevent with reasonable care. Affirmed.

Why it matters: If an equally likely cause lies outside the defendant's control, the inference fails.

cases.name: Cruz v. DaimlerChrysler Motors Corp.
cases.title: Cruz v. DaimlerChrysler Motors Corp. (R.I. 2013) — negligence must point to this defendant
cases.html:
main case

Cruz v. DaimlerChrysler Motors Corp. (R.I. 2013) — negligence must point to this defendant

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G

Facts: Cruz was cleaning out his minivan when its front airbags suddenly deployed and injured him. He sued the maker, DaimlerChrysler, and Ricky Smith Pontiac, the dealer that had sold him the van three years earlier. After DaimlerChrysler went bankrupt, he dropped it and pressed negligence claims against the dealer, relying on res ipsa loquitur. The trial court granted summary judgment for the dealer.

Held: Indeglia, J.: under R2d § 328D, element (a) was met, since airbags do not ordinarily deploy during cleaning without negligence. But element (b) failed: after three years in Cruz's hands, the evidence did not eliminate other causes or point the negligence to the dealer. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Element (b) of § 328D is the hurdle: other responsible causes must be sufficiently eliminated.

cases.name: James v. Wormuth
cases.title: James v. Wormuth (N.Y. 2013) — deliberate medical judgment
cases.html:
main case

James v. Wormuth (N.Y. 2013) — deliberate medical judgment

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G

Facts: During a procedure to biopsy a lung nodule, a guide wire Dr. Wormuth had placed became dislodged. He searched for it by hand for about 20 minutes, could not find it, and decided to end the operation rather than keep James under anesthesia longer and enlarge the incision. He told her afterward. Weeks later, when she complained of pain, he removed it in a second operation. She sued for malpractice but offered no expert testimony that leaving the wire departed from accepted practice, relying on res ipsa. The trial court granted judgment for the doctor.

Held: Rivera, J.: res ipsa applies to foreign objects left in the body unintentionally. It does not apply when the doctor deliberately left the object based on his judgment that doing so was in the patient's best interest. That judgment must be challenged with expert testimony on the standard of care. Exclusive control was also lacking, since other staff had handled the wire. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Res ipsa applies to forgotten sponges, not to deliberate choices. Those require expert proof.

cases.name: Sullivan v. Crabtree
cases.title: Sullivan v. Crabtree (Tenn. App. 1953) — procedural effect: permissible inference
cases.html:
main case

Sullivan v. Crabtree (Tenn. App. 1953) — procedural effect: permissible inference

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G

Facts: Sullivan, the plaintiffs' son, was a guest passenger in a truck Crabtree was driving down a mountain highway. The truck suddenly swerved from the right lane to the left, ran off the road, and overturned down a steep embankment, killing Sullivan. Crabtree testified that gravel or broken pavement might have made him lose control but could not say for sure. The jury found for Crabtree.

Held: Felts, J.: the facts made a case for res ipsa, which is evidence from which the jury may infer negligence. But res ipsa does not compel the jury to find negligence, even when the defendant cannot fully explain the accident; the jury may draw the inference it finds more probable. The verdict for Crabtree was affirmed.

Why it matters: Res ipsa usually creates a permissible inference, not a presumption, so the plaintiff can still lose.

cases.name: Ybarra v. Spangard
cases.title: Ybarra v. Spangard (Cal. 1944) — res ipsa against a surgical team
cases.html:
main case

Ybarra v. Spangard (Cal. 1944) — res ipsa against a surgical team

Source: Canvas reading (Res Ipsa module, due 10/8), from the opinion text in the course folder.

Facts: In October 1939, Dr. Tilley diagnosed Ybarra with appendicitis and arranged for Dr. Spangard to operate at a hospital owned and run by Dr. Swift. Dr. Reser, the anesthetist and Swift's employee, positioned Ybarra on the operating table, pulling him up so that the tops of his shoulders rested against two hard objects, and then anesthetized him. When Ybarra awoke the next morning, he had a sharp pain between his neck and right shoulder. It spread down his arm and led to paralysis and atrophy of the shoulder muscles. Two doctors testified the injury was traumatic, caused by pressure or strain, not by disease. Ybarra sued the doctors and nurses who had charge of him (Tilley, Spangard, Swift, Reser, and nurses Gisler and Thompson), but he could not say which one, or which instrumentality, injured him. The trial court granted nonsuits for all defendants.

Held: Gibson, C.J.: res ipsa applies. (1) The injury was to a healthy part of the body away from the operation, which ordinarily does not happen without negligence, and (2) Ybarra contributed nothing to it. As for control, the test is right of control, not actual exclusive control. Every defendant in whose custody Ybarra was placed owed him ordinary care, employers answer for their employees, and the surgeon in charge answers for those who become his temporary servants during the operation. "Where a plaintiff receives unusual injuries while unconscious and in the course of medical treatment, all those defendants who had any control over his body or the instrumentalities which might have caused the injuries may properly be called upon to meet the inference of negligence by giving an explanation of their conduct." Reversed.

Why it matters: Ybarra stretches exclusive control to a team of defendants because the unconscious patient cannot identify the wrongdoer and the evidence is in their hands. Otherwise, the court said, there would rarely be any compensation for patients injured while unconscious. Compare Larson (control shared with strangers defeats res ipsa) and Summers v. Tice (burden-shifting on causation, § 18). On retrial the defendants were found liable, and the judgment was affirmed (Ybarra v. Spangard, 93 Cal. App. 2d 43 (1949)).

cases.name: Perkins v. Texas and New Orleans R. Co.
cases.title: Perkins v. Texas and New Orleans R. Co. (La. 1962) — negligence that made no difference
cases.html:
main case

Perkins v. Texas and New Orleans R. Co. (La. 1962) — negligence that made no difference

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.A

Facts: A train going 37 mph, over the 25 mph limit through the town of Vinton, hit a car at a blind crossing, killing Perkins's decedent, a passenger in the car. The car's speed could not be determined. The evidence showed that even at 25 mph the train could not have stopped in time once the car came into view. The jury found for Perkins, and the court of appeal affirmed.

Held: Sanders, J.: negligence is not a cause in fact if the harm would have happened anyway. The engineer was negligent, but the plaintiff did not show that a slower train would have avoided the collision. Reversed; judgment for the railroad.

Why it matters: Negligence must be causally linked to the harm. A defendant is not liable for harm that due care would not have prevented.

cases.name: Reynolds v. Texas & Pac. Ry. Co.
cases.title: Reynolds v. Texas & Pac. Ry. Co. (La. 1885) — negligence that increases the chance of harm
cases.html:
main case

Reynolds v. Texas & Pac. Ry. Co. (La. 1885) — negligence that increases the chance of harm

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.A

Facts: Mrs. Reynolds, who weighed about 250 pounds, was hurried out of a brightly lit waiting room at night to catch her train and down unlit stairs to the platform. She fell and was badly hurt. The jury awarded $2,000. The railroad argued she might have fallen even if the stairs were lit.

Held: Fenner, J.: when negligence greatly multiplies the chances of an accident and is of a kind that naturally leads to it, the mere possibility that it might have happened anyway does not break the causal connection. Courts look at "the natural and ordinary course of events," not remote speculations. Affirmed.

Why it matters: The jury may infer causation from the fact that the harm is exactly what the negligence risked.

cases.name: Gentry v. Douglas Hereford Ranch, Inc.
cases.title: Gentry v. Douglas Hereford Ranch, Inc. (Mont. 1998) — no evidence of but-for cause
cases.html:
main case

Gentry v. Douglas Hereford Ranch, Inc. (Mont. 1998) — no evidence of but-for cause

Source: Canvas reading (10/8), from the opinion text in the course folder.

Facts: On November 5, 1994, Brent Bacon drove to the Douglas Hereford Ranch, owned by a company controlled by his wife's grandmother and leased to Pard Cattle Co. He planned to start the furnace in a house that his wife and her friend Barbara Gentry were going to paint, and then to go deer hunting. On the way he had fired his lever-action .30-30 at a fox, cocked another round into the chamber, and lowered the hammer onto the live round. After failing to start the furnace, he got the rifle from his car and walked back toward the house carrying it on his shoulder, with a finger on the trigger and his thumb on the hammer. As he reached the wooden steps to a deck, he stumbled and fell; the rifle went off, and the bullet struck Barbara Gentry in the head. She died 69 days later. Her husband sued the ranch and cattle companies, claiming that a loose bottom step and debris around it made Bacon fall, and that the ranch was vicariously liable as Bacon's employer. (Bacon was dismissed after filing for bankruptcy.) Bacon repeatedly testified that he did not know whether he tripped on something, missed the step, or was just clumsy. The trial court granted summary judgment for the defendants.

Held: Trieweiler, J.: negligence requires (1) duty, (2) breach, (3) causation, and (4) damages. Cause in fact is the but-for test, and because an intervening act was alleged, proximate cause was also in issue. Gentry offered no evidence that any condition of the steps caused Bacon to stumble. One statement ("I think it was the step") was contradicted by his own testimony that he did not know why he fell, and "a suspicion, regardless of how particularized it may be," does not defeat summary judgment. Nor was the ranch vicariously liable: Bacon's free help with the furnace did not make him its employee, and when he fell he had abandoned that task and was going hunting for himself. Affirmed.

Why it matters: But-for causation must be proved with evidence, not speculation about how an accident might have happened. Compare Reynolds (§ 17), where the jury could infer causation because the harm was exactly what the negligence risked. The case also previews respondeat superior (§ 31): no employment relationship, and no act within the scope of employment.

cases.name: Kramer Service, Inc. v. Wilkins
cases.title: Kramer Service, Inc. v. Wilkins (Miss. 1939) — possibility is not proof
cases.html:
main case

Kramer Service, Inc. v. Wilkins (Miss. 1939) — possibility is not proof

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.A

Facts: Wilkins, a guest at Kramer's hotel, was cut on the forehead when a piece of glass fell from a broken transom as he opened a door. The transom had been broken long enough that the hotel should have known. The wound never healed, and two years later a skin specialist found cancer at the spot. The undisputed expert testimony was that there was at most a remote possibility that the cut caused the cancer. The jury awarded damages including the cancer.

Held: Griffith, J.: a mere possibility of causation does not support a verdict. Jurors have no experience with skin cancer, so they may not reject undisputed expert testimony on its cause. Wilkins may recover for the cut but not for the cancer. Affirmed on liability; reversed and remanded on damages.

Why it matters: The more-likely-than-not threshold applies to each item of harm.

cases.name: Herskovits v. Group Health Cooperative of Puget Sound
cases.title: Herskovits v. Group Health Cooperative of Puget Sound (Wash. 1983) — loss of a chance
cases.html:
main case

Herskovits v. Group Health Cooperative of Puget Sound (Wash. 1983) — loss of a chance

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.A

Facts: Group Health's doctors failed to diagnose Herskovits's lung cancer for about six months. Expert testimony showed that the delay reduced his chance of surviving five years from 39% to 25%. He died, and his estate sued under the survival statute. The trial court granted summary judgment because the estate could not show he probably would have survived (a better than 50% chance) with timely diagnosis.

Held: Dore, J. (plurality): when a defendant's negligence substantially reduces a patient's chance of survival, the plaintiff need not show the patient probably would have survived; the reduction is enough to send causation to the jury, which decides what harm the increased risk caused. Damages are limited to those caused by the lost chance, not the death itself. Reversed.

Why it matters: This is the leading lost-chance case. The concurrence treated the lost chance itself as the injury, valued proportionally (14% of the full damages).

Concurrence (Pearson, J.): the lost chance itself is the compensable injury. Damages should be proportional: here, 14% of the full damages for death.

cases.name: Hill v. Edmonds
cases.title: Hill v. Edmonds (N.Y. App. Div. 1966) — concurrent causes
cases.html:
main case

Hill v. Edmonds (N.Y. App. Div. 1966) — concurrent causes

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.B

Facts: Bragoli left his truck parked without lights in the middle of the road on a stormy night. Edmonds, driving with Hill as a passenger, saw the truck four car lengths ahead, swerved, and hit it; she remembered nothing more. The trial court found Edmonds solely responsible and dismissed the complaint against Bragoli.

Held: When separate acts of negligence combine to produce a single injury, each tortfeasor is liable for the whole, even though his act alone might not have caused it. The accident could not have happened had Bragoli not left the unlighted truck in the road. Complaint against Bragoli reinstated; new trial ordered.

Why it matters: An indivisible injury from concurrent negligence makes each defendant jointly and severally liable (§ 29).

cases.name: Anderson v. Minneapolis, St. P. & S. St. M. Ry. Co.
cases.title: Anderson v. Minneapolis, St. P. & S. St. M. Ry. Co. (Minn. 1920) — the substantial factor test
cases.html:
main case

Anderson v. Minneapolis, St. P. & S. St. M. Ry. Co. (Minn. 1920) — the substantial factor test

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.B

Facts: A fire the railroad negligently started merged with a fire of unknown origin, and the combined fire burned Anderson's property. There was evidence that either fire alone would have destroyed it. The jury was instructed to find for Anderson if the railroad's fire was a material or substantial element in causing the damage, and it did.

Held: Lees, Commr.: if the railroad's fire was a material or substantial factor in causing the damage, the railroad is liable even if the other fire alone would have caused the same harm. Two known negligent fires would each be liable for the whole; the result should not change because the other fire's origin is unknown. Affirmed.

Why it matters: The substantial factor test fills the gap where the but-for test would let both causes off. An older Wisconsin rule (Cook v. Minneapolis, St. P. & S. Ste. M. Ry., 1898) excused the defendant when the other fire was of natural origin. Anderson and R2d § 432(2) reject that limit.

cases.name: Summers v. Tice
cases.title: Summers v. Tice (Cal. 1948) — alternative liability
cases.html:
main case

Summers v. Tice (Cal. 1948) — alternative liability

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.C

Facts: Summers went quail hunting with Tice and Simonson, who were each given instructions on safe shooting. A quail flew up between them and Summers, and both fired toward him at the same time with birdshot of the same size. One pellet hit his eye and another his lip. No one could tell whose gun fired which pellet. The trial court found both defendants negligent and liable.

Held: Carter, J.: when two defendants are both negligent and the plaintiff cannot prove which one caused his injury, the burden shifts to each defendant to prove he did not cause it. Otherwise both are jointly and severally liable. The defendants are wrongdoers, both put the plaintiff at risk, and they are better placed to explain what happened. Affirmed.

Why it matters: R2d § 433B(3). The rule needs all the possible wrongdoers before the court and proof that all of them were negligent.

cases.name: Sindell v. Abbott Laboratories
cases.title: Sindell v. Abbott Laboratories (Cal. 1980) — market share liability
cases.html:
main case

Sindell v. Abbott Laboratories (Cal. 1980) — market share liability

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.C

Facts: Sindell's mother took DES, a drug to prevent miscarriage, while pregnant with her. DES caused cancer in some daughters years later, and Sindell developed cancer. About 200 companies had made DES from an identical formula, many pharmacies kept no record of which maker's pills filled a prescription, and Sindell could not identify the maker. She sued five makers. The trial court dismissed.

Held: Mosk, J.: a plaintiff who cannot identify the maker of a fungible product through no fault of her own may recover if she joins makers of a substantial share of the market. Each defendant is liable for the share of the judgment matching its market share, unless it proves it could not have made the product that injured her. Summers v. Tice could not be applied directly, because the maker might not be before the court. Reversed.

Why it matters: Market share liability is a narrow exception, mostly limited to DES. Hymowitz v. Eli Lilly (N.Y. 1989) used a national market and did not let a defendant exculpate itself.

cases.name: Atlantic Coast Line R. Co. v. Daniels
cases.title: Atlantic Coast Line R. Co. v. Daniels (Ga. App. 1911) — the need for a limit
cases.html:
main case

Atlantic Coast Line R. Co. v. Daniels (Ga. App. 1911) — the need for a limit

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.A

Facts: The opinion discusses the concept in general terms, without a fact pattern the casebook relies on.

Held: Every act has endless consequences, so the law must draw a practical, somewhat arbitrary line. Words like "proximate" and "natural" describe where courts stop tracing the connection between a wrongful act and an injury.

Why it matters: Proximate cause is a policy judgment about the limits of responsibility.

cases.name: Ryan v. New York Central R.R. Co.
cases.title: Ryan v. New York Central R.R. Co. (N.Y. 1866) — the old first-house rule
cases.html:
main case

Ryan v. New York Central R.R. Co. (N.Y. 1866) — the old first-house rule

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.A

Facts: A spark from the railroad's engine in Syracuse set fire to its own woodshed, through careless management or the engine's poor condition. The fire spread to Ryan's house, 130 feet away, and destroyed it, along with several other houses. The trial court nonsuited Ryan.

Held: Hunt, J.: the railroad was liable only to the owner of the first building burned. The spread of fire to other buildings is not a necessary or usual result of a spark, and liability for every building a fire reaches would be ruinous; everyone runs some risk from neighbors and can insure. Affirmed.

Why it matters: This rule has been abandoned. Today the spread of fire is a foreseeable consequence. It shows how policy (a new industry, insurance, ruinous liability) drives proximate cause.

cases.name: Bartolone v. Jeckovich
cases.title: Bartolone v. Jeckovich (N.Y. App. Div. 1984) — the eggshell plaintiff
cases.html:
main case

Bartolone v. Jeckovich (N.Y. App. Div. 1984) — the eggshell plaintiff

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.A

Facts: Bartolone, a bodybuilder, suffered minor neck and back injuries in a car accident caused by Jeckovich. He then had a complete psychotic breakdown. Experts testified that he had a traumatic childhood and had used bodybuilding and a strict regimen to cope, and that when the accident disrupted his routine, his latent condition broke down. The jury awarded $500,000, but the trial court set the verdict aside as unsupported.

Held: Denman, J.: a defendant takes the plaintiff as he finds him and is liable for all damages proximately caused, even if they seem out of proportion to the incident because of a pre-existing condition. The jury was entitled to believe the testimony that the accident triggered his breakdown. Reversed; verdict reinstated.

Why it matters: The eggshell plaintiff rule covers the extent of harm, including psychological harm. It is the clearest exception to foreseeability.

cases.name: Polemis v. Furness, Withy & Co.
cases.title: Polemis v. Furness, Withy & Co. (C.A. 1921) — direct consequences
cases.html:
main case

Polemis v. Furness, Withy & Co. (C.A. 1921) — direct consequences

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B

Facts: Reported as In re Arbitration Between Polemis and Furness, Withy & Co. Furness chartered the ship Polemis, which carried petrol and benzine. While unloading at Casablanca, stevedores employed by the charterers carelessly let a plank fall into the hold. It struck something and caused a spark, which ignited petrol vapor, and the ship was destroyed. The arbitrators found that a spark could not reasonably have been anticipated, but that some damage to the ship from the falling plank could have been.

Held: Once an act is negligent, the defendant is liable for all the direct consequences, even those that could not reasonably have been anticipated, so long as they are not due to an independent cause. Because some damage from dropping the plank was foreseeable, the fire was a direct result for which the charterers were liable.

Why it matters: This is the direct-consequences test, which Wagon Mound No. 1 rejected.

cases.name: Overseas Tankship v. Morts Dock
cases.title: Overseas Tankship v. Morts Dock (P.C. 1961) — Wagon Mound No. 1: foreseeable kind of harm
cases.html:
main case

Overseas Tankship v. Morts Dock (P.C. 1961) — Wagon Mound No. 1: foreseeable kind of harm

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B

Facts: The Wagon Mound, moored about 600 feet from Morts Dock's wharf in Sydney Harbour, carelessly discharged a large quantity of furnace oil. The oil spread to the wharf, where Morts Dock's workers were welding. Two days later molten metal from the welding fell onto cotton waste floating on the oil, which ignited the oil, and the wharf burned. The trial court found that Overseas did not know, and could not reasonably have known, that furnace oil (flash point about 170°F) would burn when spread on water. It nonetheless found for Morts Dock under Polemis.

Held: Viscount Simonds: Polemis is no longer good law. It is not consistent with justice that a negligent actor be liable for all consequences, however unforeseeable and grave, merely because they are "direct." Liability is limited to damage of the kind a reasonable person would have foreseen. Fouling of the wharf was foreseeable; fire was not. Reversed.

Why it matters: The foreseeable-type-of-harm test. Liability matches the risk that made the conduct negligent.

cases.name: Overseas Tankship v. Miller Steamship Co.
cases.title: Overseas Tankship v. Miller Steamship Co. (P.C. 1967) — Wagon Mound No. 2: small but real risk
cases.html:
main case

Overseas Tankship v. Miller Steamship Co. (P.C. 1967) — Wagon Mound No. 2: small but real risk

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B

Facts: The same fire damaged two ships owned by Miller Steamship that were being refitted at the wharf. On different evidence, the trial court found that the Wagon Mound's officers would have regarded fire as a possibility, though it would occur only in very exceptional circumstances, and it held for the defendant on the ground that the damage was not reasonably foreseeable.

Held: Lord Reid: a reasonable person would not ignore a real risk, even a small one, if it could be eliminated easily and there was no valid reason for running it. Discharging oil into the harbor was unjustified, and the engineer should have known fire was possible, so the risk, though slight, made the defendant liable. Reversed; judgment for Miller.

Why it matters: This is the same accident with a different result, because foreseeability is a finding of fact and it ties back to the Hand formula (§ 11).

cases.name: Palsgraf v. Long Island R.R. Co.
cases.title: Palsgraf v. Long Island R.R. Co. (N.Y. 1928) — the unforeseeable plaintiff
cases.html:
main case

Palsgraf v. Long Island R.R. Co. (N.Y. 1928) — the unforeseeable plaintiff

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B

Facts: Mrs. Palsgraf bought a ticket to Rockaway Beach and was standing on the platform. Two men ran to catch a train that was pulling out. One guard on the train pulled and another on the platform pushed one of them aboard. He was carrying a small package wrapped in newspaper, which fell onto the rails. It contained fireworks and exploded. The shock knocked over scales at the far end of the platform, which struck Mrs. Palsgraf. The jury found for her, and the Appellate Division affirmed.

Held: Cardozo, C.J.: "The risk reasonably to be perceived defines the duty to be obeyed." Negligence is not a tort in the abstract; it is a wrong only to someone within the range of apparent danger. Nothing about the package suggested danger to a person standing far away, so the guards' conduct, even if negligent toward the man or his package, was not a wrong toward Mrs. Palsgraf. Reversed; complaint dismissed.

Why it matters: The leading case on unforeseeable plaintiffs. Cardozo frames it as duty (the zone of danger), Andrews as proximate cause.

Dissent (Andrews, J.): everyone owes the world at large a duty to refrain from acts that unreasonably threaten others. When an act is negligent, the defendant is liable for the injuries it proximately causes, and proximate cause is a practical line drawn by "convenience, of public policy, of a rough sense of justice." Factors include a natural and continuous sequence, direct connection, foreseeability, and remoteness in time and space. Here the explosion's effect was close and direct, and he would have affirmed.

cases.name: Yun v. Ford Motor Co.
cases.title: Yun v. Ford Motor Co. (N.J. Super. App. Div. 1994) — plaintiff's own conduct as the sole proximate cause
cases.html:
main case

Yun v. Ford Motor Co. (N.J. Super. App. Div. 1994) — plaintiff's own conduct as the sole proximate cause

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B

Facts: Chang was a passenger in a 1987 Ford van his daughter Yun was driving on the Garden State Parkway at night. The spare tire assembly fell off the back and rolled across both lanes to the guardrail. Yun pulled over on the right shoulder. Chang ran across the Parkway to retrieve the tire and was struck and killed by another car. Yun sued Ford and others, alleging a defective spare tire bracket. The trial court granted summary judgment.

Held: Villanueva, J.: even assuming a defect, Chang's decision to cross a busy highway at night to retrieve a spare tire was so extraordinary and unforeseeable that it was the sole proximate cause of his death. Affirmed. The New Jersey Supreme Court reversed, substantially for the reasons of the Appellate Division dissent, which would let a jury decide whether his response was foreseeable (143 N.J. 162 (1996)).

Why it matters: A plaintiff's extraordinary response can cut off proximate cause. Many courts leave the question to the jury and handle it as comparative fault.

cases.name: Derdiarian v. Felix Contracting Corp.
cases.title: Derdiarian v. Felix Contracting Corp. (N.Y. 1980) — intervening act within the risk
cases.html:
main case

Derdiarian v. Felix Contracting Corp. (N.Y. 1980) — intervening act within the risk

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C

Facts: Felix, a general contractor, was installing a gas main and had an excavation on one side of a road. It set up no adequate barrier. Derdiarian, a subcontractor's employee, was working beside a kettle of 400-degree liquid enamel. Dickens, who had not taken his epilepsy medication, had a seizure while driving, lost control, and crashed into the work site. Derdiarian was thrown into the air and splashed with the burning enamel. The jury found against Felix.

Held: Cooke, C.J.: an intervening act does not break the causal chain if it is a normal or foreseeable consequence of the situation the defendant's negligence created. The very reason Felix's failure to barricade was negligent was the risk of a car entering the site. That the risk materialized in an unusual way, or that the driver was also negligent, does not relieve Felix. Proximate cause was properly left to the jury. Affirmed.

Why it matters: If the intervening act is within the risk, it does not supersede. Proximate cause is usually a jury question.

cases.name: Watson v. Kentucky & Indiana Bridge & R.R. Co.
cases.title: Watson v. Kentucky & Indiana Bridge & R.R. Co. (Ky. 1910) — negligent vs. malicious intervention
cases.html:
main case

Watson v. Kentucky & Indiana Bridge & R.R. Co. (Ky. 1910) — negligent vs. malicious intervention

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C

Facts: Through the railroad's negligence, a tank car full of gasoline derailed, its valve broke, and gasoline poured into the street. Duerr struck a match, igniting the vapor, and the explosion injured Watson. There was conflicting evidence whether Duerr lit the match to light his cigar or did it deliberately to cause an explosion. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad.

Held: Settle, J.: the jury should have decided why Duerr lit the match. If he did it inadvertently, his act was a foreseeable consequence of the spill and the railroad remains liable. If he did it maliciously, the railroad could not reasonably have anticipated it, and his act is the sole proximate cause. Reversed; new trial.

Why it matters: The traditional rule is that foreseeable negligence of a third person does not supersede, but a deliberate crime does. R2d § 448 moderates this when the defendant's negligence created the opportunity for the crime.

cases.name: Fuller v. Preis
cases.title: Fuller v. Preis (N.Y. 1974) — suicide as an irresistible impulse
cases.html:
main case

Fuller v. Preis (N.Y. 1974) — suicide as an irresistible impulse

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C

Facts: Dr. Lewis, a surgeon, suffered head injuries in a car accident caused by Preis. He had been healthy before. Afterward he had 38 epileptic seizures, three on the day of his death, which drugs could not control. He became depressed, unsteady, and irritable, and seven months after the accident he shot himself, leaving notes saying he was sane. A neurologist testified he was in a post-seizure psychosis that put his conduct beyond his control. The jury awarded $200,000, but the Appellate Division reversed and dismissed.

Held: Breitel, C.J.: suicide is not a superseding cause as a matter of law. A tortfeasor is liable for a suicide that results from an irresistible impulse caused by the injury, even if the decedent understood what he was doing. His notes declaring his sanity were not conclusive. The evidence supported the jury's finding. Reversed.

Why it matters: The defendant's tort created the mental condition, so the plaintiff's act is not a free, informed choice that cuts off liability.

cases.name: McCoy v. American Suzuki Motor Corp.
cases.title: McCoy v. American Suzuki Motor Corp. (Wash. 1998) — the rescue doctrine
cases.html:
main case

McCoy v. American Suzuki Motor Corp. (Wash. 1998) — the rescue doctrine

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C

Facts: McCoy was driving on an interstate at night when the Suzuki Samurai ahead of him swerved off the road and rolled. He stopped to help and found the driver badly hurt. A state trooper asked him to set out flares. After the injured were cared for, McCoy was walking back to his car along the road when a hit-and-run driver struck him. He sued Suzuki, claiming the Samurai was defectively prone to roll over. The trial court granted summary judgment for Suzuki. The court of appeals reversed, holding that a rescuer need only show the defendant caused the danger.

Held: Sanders, J.: the rescue doctrine applies in products cases. "Danger invites rescue," so a rescuer is a foreseeable plaintiff, and the rescuer is not presumed to have assumed the risk unless he acted rashly. But the doctrine does not relieve the rescuer of proving proximate cause of his own injuries. Whether Suzuki's defect proximately caused McCoy's injuries was a fact question, so summary judgment was improper. Court of appeals affirmed on different grounds.

Why it matters: A rescuer is a foreseeable plaintiff. To invoke the doctrine, the rescuer shows all required:
(1) the defendant's negligence (or defect) caused the peril;
(2) the peril was imminent;
(3) a reasonably prudent person would have concluded that the peril existed; and
(4) the rescuer acted with reasonable care in carrying out the rescue.

cases.name: Kelly v. Gwinnell
cases.title: Kelly v. Gwinnell (N.J. 1984) — social host liability
cases.html:
main case

Kelly v. Gwinnell (N.J. 1984) — social host liability

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C

Facts: Gwinnell drank at Zak's home and, according to the complaint, Zak served him until he was visibly intoxicated, then accompanied him to his car, chatted, and watched him drive off. Gwinnell's blood-alcohol level was later 0.286. He collided head-on with Kelly's car. Kelly sued Gwinnell and Zak. The trial court granted summary judgment for Zak, and the Appellate Division affirmed.

Held: Wilentz, C.J.: a social host who directly serves liquor to an adult guest, knowing the guest is intoxicated and will soon drive, is liable to third parties injured by the guest's drunk driving. The law already made commercial servers and hosts serving minors liable, and the risk is foreseeable. The guest's drunk driving is not a superseding cause. Reversed. (The rule was applied prospectively.)

Why it matters: This is the minority rule. Many legislatures, including California's, have rejected it, and the dissent said the legislature should decide. Delaware recognizes no dram shop or social host liability (McCall v. Villa Pizza, Del. 1994).

Dissent (Garibaldi, J.): the competing social and economic interests (insurance, the burden on hosts) should be weighed by the legislature, not imposed by the court.

cases.name: Enright v. Eli Lilly & Co.
cases.title: Enright v. Eli Lilly & Co. (N.Y. 1991) — policy limit: third-generation DES claims
cases.html:
main case

Enright v. Eli Lilly & Co. (N.Y. 1991) — policy limit: third-generation DES claims

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C

Facts: In 1960, Enright's grandmother took DES while pregnant with Enright's mother, Patricia. DES allegedly damaged Patricia's reproductive system in utero. Enright was born prematurely, with cerebral palsy and other disabilities, allegedly as a result. She sued Eli Lilly. The trial court dismissed her claim; the Appellate Division affirmed.

Held: Wachtler, C.J.: a child injured because of a tort to her mother before the child was conceived has no claim against the original tortfeasor. Liability to those who took the drug or were exposed in utero serves deterrence; extending it to later generations would create staggering, open-ended liability and could deter drug development. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Courts sometimes cut off liability for policy reasons, even where harm is foreseeable and causation is clear.

cases.name: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.
cases.title: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. (N.Y. 1916) — the end of the privity limit
cases.html:
main case

MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. (N.Y. 1916) — the end of the privity limit

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.A

Facts: Buick sold a car to a retail dealer, who sold it to MacPherson. While he was driving, one of the wooden wheels collapsed because its spokes were made of defective wood, and he was thrown out and injured. Another company made the wheel, but a reasonable inspection by Buick would have revealed the defect. The jury found for MacPherson, and the Appellate Division affirmed.

Held: Cardozo, J.: if a product is reasonably certain to place life and limb in peril when negligently made, and the maker knows it will be used by people other than the buyer without new tests, the maker owes those users a duty of care, regardless of privity. Buick was a manufacturer of finished cars and could not escape its duty to inspect components. Affirmed.

Why it matters: MacPherson rejected Winterbottom v. Wright (1842), which required privity. A negligent manufacturer owes a duty to foreseeable users.

cases.name: H.R. Moch Co. v. Rensselaer Water Co.
cases.title: H.R. Moch Co. v. Rensselaer Water Co. (N.Y. 1928) — nonfeasance in performing a contract
cases.html:
main case

H.R. Moch Co. v. Rensselaer Water Co. (N.Y. 1928) — nonfeasance in performing a contract

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.A

Facts: The water company contracted with the City of Rensselaer to supply water for fire hydrants, public buildings, and private customers. A fire spread from a nearby building to Moch's warehouse. The company was promptly notified but failed to supply enough water pressure at the hydrants, and the warehouse burned. Moch sued for breach of contract, common-law tort, and breach of statutory duty.

Held: Cardozo, C.J.: the company owed no tort duty to individual citizens. Its failure was the withholding of a benefit (nonfeasance), not the launching of "a force or an instrument of harm" (misfeasance). Citizens were only incidental beneficiaries of the contract, and recognizing the claim would make suppliers liable to an indefinite number of people. Dismissal affirmed.

Why it matters: The test: has the defendant "launched a force or instrument of harm," or only failed to confer a benefit? Policy concerns about unlimited liability also played a role.

cases.name: Clagett v. Dacy
cases.title: Clagett v. Dacy (Md. Ct. Spec. App. 1980) — lawyer's duty to non-clients
cases.html:
main case

Clagett v. Dacy (Md. Ct. Spec. App. 1980) — lawyer's duty to non-clients

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.A

Facts: Dacy, an attorney, was hired by a mortgage lender to conduct a foreclosure sale. Because he did not follow proper procedures, the sale was set aside twice, and during the delay the borrower paid off the loan and redeemed the property. Clagett, the high bidder at both sales, sued Dacy for malpractice, claiming he lost a chance to buy the land and resell it at a profit. The trial court sustained Dacy's demurrer.

Held: Wilner, J.: a lawyer owes no duty of care to a third party with whom he has no attorney-client relationship, unless the third party is an intended beneficiary of the representation, such as a will beneficiary. Bidders at a foreclosure sale are adverse to the lender's lawyer, who seeks the highest price while bidders seek the lowest. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Privity still limits professional malpractice duties for economic loss, subject to the third-party-beneficiary exception.

cases.name: L.S. Ayres & Co. v. Hicks
cases.title: L.S. Ayres & Co. v. Hicks (Ind. 1942) — duty to aid a business invitee
cases.html:
main case

L.S. Ayres & Co. v. Hicks (Ind. 1942) — duty to aid a business invitee

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B

Facts: Hicks, a six-year-old boy shopping with his mother at the Ayres department store, fell on an escalator and caught his fingers in the moving parts. Store employees did not stop the escalator for an unreasonable time, and his injuries were made worse. The jury found the store liable for all his injuries.

Held: Shake, C.J.: a store that invites customers onto its premises and controls the instrumentality that injured one of them must use reasonable care to aid the injured invitee, even if the store did not cause the original injury and the invitee was careless. But the store is liable only for the aggravation caused by its failure to act, not for the original injury. Reversed; new trial.

Why it matters: This is the business-invitee exception. Liability is limited to harm caused by the failure to act.

cases.name: Hegel v. Langsam
cases.title: Hegel v. Langsam (Ohio C.P. 1971) — no duty to supervise adult students
cases.html:
main case

Hegel v. Langsam (Ohio C.P. 1971) — no duty to supervise adult students

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B

Facts: The Hegels' 17-year-old daughter enrolled as a freshman at the University of Cincinnati and was assigned to a dormitory. The university did not monitor her comings and goings. She stopped staying in the dormitory, became involved with criminals, was seduced, and began using drugs. Her parents demanded the university return her, but officials could not. The parents sued for failure to supervise.

Held: Bettman, J.: a university has no duty to regulate the private lives of its students, control their comings and goings, or supervise their associations. It is an educational institution, not a nursery, boarding school, or prison, and students are presumed mature enough to care for themselves. Judgment on the pleadings for the university.

Why it matters: There is no general custodial relationship between a college and adult students.

cases.name: Commonwealth v. Peterson
cases.title: Commonwealth v. Peterson (Va. 2013) — duty to warn of crime
cases.html:
main case

Commonwealth v. Peterson (Va. 2013) — duty to warn of crime

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B

Facts: At about 7:15 a.m. on April 16, 2007, a gunman shot two students in West Ambler Johnston Hall at Virginia Tech, killing one. Police concluded it was a targeted domestic homicide, that the shooter had probably fled, and that a lockdown was unnecessary; they pursued a person of interest, a victim's boyfriend. University administrators sent a campus email about the shooting at 9:26 a.m. Around 9:40 a.m., the same gunman began shooting in Norris Hall, killing 30 more people, including Erin Peterson and Julia Pryde. Their estates sued the Commonwealth, and a jury found it negligent for failing to warn students sooner.

Held: Powell, J.: assuming without deciding that a special relationship existed between the university and its students, there was no duty to warn of third-party criminal harm unless the harm was known or reasonably foreseeable. Based on what officials knew before the second shooting (a targeted killing, a shooter who had apparently fled), it was not reasonably foreseeable that students in classroom buildings would be harmed. Reversed; final judgment for the Commonwealth.

Why it matters: Even where a special relationship exists, the duty extends only to foreseeable harm. Foreseeability usually requires knowledge of an imminent probability of injury.

cases.name: J.S. v. R.T.H.
cases.title: J.S. v. R.T.H. (N.J. 1998) — duty to protect from a spouse's abuse
cases.html:
main case

J.S. v. R.T.H. (N.J. 1998) — duty to protect from a spouse's abuse

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B

Facts: Two young sisters spent a great deal of time with their neighbor, R.T.H., at his horse barn. He sexually abused them over a period of time. Their parents sued him and his wife, claiming she knew or should have known of his conduct. The trial court granted summary judgment for the wife; the Appellate Division reversed.

Held: Handler, J.: when a spouse has actual knowledge or special reason to know that her spouse is likely to abuse a particular person, she has a duty of reasonable care to prevent or warn of the abuse, and a breach can be a proximate cause of it. The court weighed foreseeability (the most important factor), the severity of the harm, the opportunity to prevent it, the parties' relationships, and public policy against child abuse. Affirmed; case remanded for trial.

Why it matters: The duty is based on foreseeability, the relationship, and strong public policy against child abuse.

cases.name: Tarasoff v. Regents of University of California
cases.title: Tarasoff v. Regents of University of California (Cal. 1976) — therapist's duty to protect third persons
cases.html:
main case

Tarasoff v. Regents of University of California (Cal. 1976) — therapist's duty to protect third persons

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B

Facts: Prosenjit Poddar, a patient at the university's hospital, told his psychologist, Dr. Moore, that he intended to kill Tatiana Tarasoff, an identifiable young woman who had rejected him. Dr. Moore notified campus police and asked that Poddar be detained. Police held him briefly but released him when he seemed rational, and the psychiatry director ordered no further action. No one warned Tarasoff or her family. Two months later Poddar killed her. Her parents sued; the trial court sustained demurrers.

Held: Tobriner, J.: when a therapist determines, or under the standards of the profession should determine, that a patient presents a serious danger of violence to another, the therapist must use reasonable care to protect the intended victim, by warning her, notifying the police, or taking other reasonable steps. The special relationship with the patient supports the duty. Confidentiality must yield: "The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins." The complaint stated a cause of action against the therapists (the police were immune).

Why it matters: The special relationship with a dangerous person supports a duty to an identifiable victim. Most states now codify and limit the duty by statute, often to a serious threat against a reasonably identifiable victim.

cases.name: Butterfield v. Forrester
cases.title: Butterfield v. Forrester (K.B. 1809) — contributory negligence as a bar
cases.html:
main case

Butterfield v. Forrester (K.B. 1809) — contributory negligence as a bar

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.A

Facts: Forrester, repairing his house, put a pole across part of the road, though passage was still possible. At dusk, when candles were just being lit but a rider could see 100 yards ahead, Butterfield rode out "violently," did not see the pole, crashed into it, and was thrown and injured. There was no evidence he was drunk. The jury found for Forrester.

Held: Lord Ellenborough, C.J.: a plaintiff cannot recover when his own lack of ordinary care contributed to the accident. "One person being in fault will not dispense with another's using ordinary care for himself." Had Butterfield ridden with ordinary care, he would have seen the pole. Judgment for Forrester.

Why it matters: This is the origin of the all-or-nothing contributory negligence bar.

cases.name: Davies v. Mann
cases.title: Davies v. Mann (Ex. 1842) — last clear chance
cases.html:
main case

Davies v. Mann (Ex. 1842) — last clear chance

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.A

Facts: Davies fettered the forefeet of his donkey and turned it onto a narrow public road to graze. Mann's wagon, driven at a "smartish pace" by a servant who was not watching, knocked it down and killed it.

Held: Lord Abinger, C.B., and Parke, B.: Davies's negligence in leaving the donkey on the road does not bar recovery, because Mann could have avoided the accident with ordinary care. Otherwise a driver could run over anything lawfully or unlawfully in the road. Verdict for Davies upheld.

Why it matters: This is the origin of last clear chance, the main escape from the contributory negligence bar. R2d §§ 479–480 distinguish a helpless plaintiff (the defendant is liable if it knew or should have known) from an inattentive one (the defendant is liable only if it actually knew).

cases.name: McIntyre v. Balentine
cases.title: McIntyre v. Balentine (Tenn. 1992) — adopting modified comparative fault
cases.html:
main case

McIntyre v. Balentine (Tenn. 1992) — adopting modified comparative fault

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.A

Facts: McIntyre and Balentine collided at night on a highway. Both had been drinking, and there was evidence Balentine was speeding. The jury, instructed on contributory negligence, found them equally at fault, which barred McIntyre.

Held: Drowota, J.: Tennessee abolishes contributory negligence and adopts modified comparative fault. A plaintiff may recover so long as her fault is less than the defendants' combined fault (the 49% bar), with damages reduced by her percentage. Last clear chance, remote contributory negligence, and joint and several liability are rendered obsolete. The jury might have apportioned fault differently under the new rule, so a new trial was ordered.

Why it matters: This is the 49% bar version of modified comparative fault, adopted by a court rather than a legislature. Compare Li v. Yellow Cab (Cal. 1975), which adopted pure comparative fault.

cases.name: Seigneur v. National Fitness Institute, Inc.
cases.title: Seigneur v. National Fitness Institute, Inc. (Md. Ct. Spec. App. 2000) — exculpatory clause in a gym contract
cases.html:
main case

Seigneur v. National Fitness Institute, Inc. (Md. Ct. Spec. App. 2000) — exculpatory clause in a gym contract

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.B

Facts: Gerilynne Seigneur joined NFI's gym and signed a membership agreement in which she assumed "all risk of injury" from using the facilities and released NFI from all claims, expressly including its negligence. At her initial evaluation, she hurt her right shoulder on a weight machine. She and her husband sued for negligence, both vicarious (the employee's evaluation) and direct (negligent hiring and training). The trial court granted summary judgment for NFI.

Held: Salmon, J.: an exculpatory clause is valid if it clearly and specifically releases the defendant from liability for its own negligence, unless (1) the conduct was intentional, reckless, wanton, or grossly negligent; (2) the bargaining power was grossly unequal; or (3) the transaction affects the public interest. The agreement was an adhesion contract, but that alone does not show grossly unequal bargaining power: Seigneur could have gone to another gym for a non-essential service. Health clubs are not in the public-interest category. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Recreational releases are usually enforced. Releases in medical care, public utilities, and similar essential services usually are not.

cases.name: Rush v. Commercial Realty Co.
cases.title: Rush v. Commercial Realty Co. (N.J. 1929) — no voluntary choice
cases.html:
main case

Rush v. Commercial Realty Co. (N.J. 1929) — no voluntary choice

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.B

Facts: Rush rented a house from Commercial Realty, which provided an outhouse as the only toilet for its tenants. Rush knew the floor was in bad condition. When she used it, she fell through a trap door in the floor into the pit below. The jury found for Rush, and the landlord appealed the denial of its motions for nonsuit and directed verdict.

Held: Per curiam: assumption of risk requires a free and voluntary choice. Rush had no reasonable alternative to using the only toilet provided, and she was not required to leave her home and go elsewhere. Whether stepping on a floor she knew was in poor repair was contributory negligence was for the jury, but it was not assumption of risk. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Voluntariness requires a genuine choice. A choice the defendant forces on the plaintiff does not count.

cases.name: Blackburn v. Dorta
cases.title: Blackburn v. Dorta (Fla. 1977) — merging implied assumption of risk into comparative fault
cases.html:
main case

Blackburn v. Dorta (Fla. 1977) — merging implied assumption of risk into comparative fault

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.B

Facts: The court consolidated several cases, including car-accident cases, raising the same question: whether implied assumption of risk survived as a complete defense after Florida adopted comparative negligence in Hoffman v. Jones (1973).

Held: Sundberg, J.: assumption of risk is a confused doctrine with many labels: express and implied, primary and secondary, strict ("pure") and qualified. Only implied, secondary, qualified assumption of risk has mattered as a defense, and it is indistinguishable from contributory negligence. It is therefore merged into comparative negligence and is no longer a complete bar. Express assumption of risk and the no-duty situations covered by primary assumption of risk are unaffected.

Why it matters: This is the standard way courts sort the doctrine. The labels confuse; ask whether there was a duty and whether the plaintiff acted unreasonably.

cases.name: Teeters v. Currey
cases.title: Teeters v. Currey (Tenn. 1974) — the discovery rule in malpractice
cases.html:
main case

Teeters v. Currey (Tenn. 1974) — the discovery rule in malpractice

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.C

Facts: On June 5, 1970, after delivering Mrs. Teeters's child, Dr. Currey performed a bilateral tubal ligation to prevent future pregnancies. On December 6, 1972, she learned she was pregnant again, and on March 9, 1973, she delivered a premature child with severe complications. She sued on November 15, 1973. Currey pleaded the one-year statute of limitations, and the trial court agreed.

Held: Henry, J.: in a malpractice action for negligent surgery, the limitations period begins when the patient discovers, or in the exercise of reasonable care should have discovered, the injury, not on the date of the operation. It would be unfair to bar a claim before the patient could know of it. Teeters sued within a year of discovery. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: This is a judicial adoption of the discovery rule. Many legislatures responded with medical malpractice statutes of repose that cap the discovery period.

cases.name: Freehe v. Freehe
cases.title: Freehe v. Freehe (Wash. 1972) — abolishing interspousal immunity
cases.html:
main case

Freehe v. Freehe (Wash. 1972) — abolishing interspousal immunity

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D

Facts: Clifford Freehe was injured by a tractor that his wife, Hazel, owned as her separate property and kept on her separate farm. He sued her for negligently maintaining the tractor and failing to warn him of its condition. The trial court granted summary judgment for Hazel on interspousal immunity.

Held: Neill, J.: interspousal immunity in personal injury cases is abolished. Its rationales fail: (1) husband and wife are no longer one legal person; (2) a suit will not disrupt a harmonious marriage, since spouses at peace will not sue or will drop the suit; and (3) criminal and divorce law do not compensate for injuries. Fraud and collusion are policed by the ordinary trial process. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: This reflects the national trend. Fraud concerns are handled by the ordinary trial process and insurance law, not by a blanket bar.

cases.name: Zellmer v. Zellmer
cases.title: Zellmer v. Zellmer (Wash. 2008) — parental immunity and stepparents
cases.html:
main case

Zellmer v. Zellmer (Wash. 2008) — parental immunity and stepparents

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D

Facts: Three-year-old Ashley McLellan lived with her mother and her stepfather, Mr. Zellmer. While he was watching her, he started a video for her and went downstairs to build a fire. About an hour later he found the sliding door to the backyard open and Ashley floating in the pool. She was resuscitated but died two days later. Her mother and biological father sued him for wrongful death. He moved for summary judgment, claiming parental immunity because he stood in loco parentis. The trial court and court of appeals agreed with him.

Held: Madsen, J.: Washington keeps parental immunity for negligent parental supervision, but it does not extend to a stepparent or anyone else who is not a biological or adoptive parent, even one acting in loco parentis. A stepparent does not acquire parental rights or obligations merely by the relationship. The stepfather is held to ordinary care. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: Courts read the remaining family immunities narrowly.

cases.name: Abernathy v. Sisters of St. Mary's
cases.title: Abernathy v. Sisters of St. Mary's (Mo. 1969) — abolishing charitable immunity
cases.html:
main case

Abernathy v. Sisters of St. Mary's (Mo. 1969) — abolishing charitable immunity

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D

Facts: Abernathy, a patient at the Sisters of St. Mary's hospital, a charitable institution, was injured when a hospital employee negligently failed to help him as he moved from his bed to the bathroom. The trial court granted the hospital summary judgment on charitable immunity.

Held: Henley, C.J.: charitable immunity is abolished. A charitable institution is liable for its own negligence and for its employees' negligence within the scope of their employment. Immunity "fosters neglect and breeds irresponsibility, while liability promotes care and caution," and modern charity is big business that can insure. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: Almost every state has abolished or limited charitable immunity. Some states cap damages against charities or limit recovery to insurance.

cases.name: Deuser v. Vecera
cases.title: Deuser v. Vecera (8th Cir. 1998) — FTCA discretionary function
cases.html:
main case

Deuser v. Vecera (8th Cir. 1998) — FTCA discretionary function

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D

Facts: Deuser attended the Veiled Prophet Fair on the grounds of the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial (the Gateway Arch) in St. Louis, a national park. Park rangers saw him grabbing women and urinating in public, arrested him, and turned him over to St. Louis police, who decided not to hold him. He was released in a parking lot, with no money or transportation, and later wandered onto an interstate and was struck and killed. His survivors sued the United States under the FTCA. The district court dismissed.

Held: Bowman, J.: the discretionary function exception bars claims based on conduct that (1) involves an element of judgment or choice, and (2) is of the kind the exception was meant to shield, grounded in social, economic, or political policy. No mandatory policy dictated how the rangers had to handle a drunk, disorderly visitor; their choices to arrest him and turn him over to local police involved judgments about law enforcement priorities and resources. Affirmed.

Why it matters: The exception sweeps in many operational law enforcement decisions, not just high-level policy.

cases.name: Clarke v. Oregon Health Sciences University
cases.title: Clarke v. Oregon Health Sciences University (Or. 2007) — limits on legislated immunity
cases.html:
main case

Clarke v. Oregon Health Sciences University (Or. 2007) — limits on legislated immunity

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D

Facts: Jordaan Clarke, an infant, had surgery at the state-run Oregon Health Sciences University to repair a congenital heart defect. Through employees' negligence, he suffered prolonged oxygen deprivation and permanent brain damage, leaving him totally disabled. He sought more than $17 million. The Oregon Tort Claims Act capped damages against the state at $200,000 and made the suit against the public body the exclusive remedy, barring claims against the individual employees. The trial court entered judgment for $200,000 against OHSU and dismissed the employees; the court of appeals reversed as to the employees.

Held: De Muniz, C.J.: the remedy clause of the Oregon Constitution (Art. I, § 10) guarantees "remedy by due course of law for injury done" to person or property. Eliminating the claim against the negligent employees and substituting a $200,000 claim against the state, against damages exceeding $17 million, left an "emasculated" remedy that is no substitute. As applied, the exclusive-remedy provision is unconstitutional, and the claims against the employees may proceed. Court of appeals affirmed.

Why it matters: State constitutions, not just legislatures, can limit how far immunity and damages caps reach.

cases.name: Riss v. City of New York
cases.title: Riss v. City of New York (N.Y. 1968) — no duty to provide police protection
cases.html:
main case

Riss v. City of New York (N.Y. 1968) — no duty to provide police protection

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D

Facts: For months, Linda Riss's rejected suitor, Burton Pugach, a lawyer, threatened to kill or maim her if she would not marry him. She repeatedly asked the police for protection and was refused. After she announced her engagement to another man, a thug hired by Pugach threw lye in her face, blinding her in one eye and permanently scarring her face. She sued the city for negligent failure to protect her. The complaint was dismissed.

Held: Breitel, J.: absent a specific legislative mandate, a municipality is not liable for its failure to provide police protection to a member of the public, even one who was specifically threatened. Allocating limited police resources is a matter for the legislative and executive branches, and liability would expose the city to unlimited claims. Affirmed.

Why it matters: The public duty doctrine. Compare Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales (U.S. 2005), which found no constitutional right to enforcement of a restraining order. It is also a bias lens: the rule falls hardest on people, often women, who depend on the police for protection from violence.

Dissent (Keating, J.): the city's immunity rests on a fiction and leaves the victim of official negligence without a remedy. The fear of crushing liability was exaggerated, and ordinary negligence principles should apply when the police ignore a known, specific threat.

cases.name: DeLong v. Erie County
cases.title: DeLong v. Erie County (N.Y. App. Div. 1982) — special duty through a 911 call
cases.html:
main case

DeLong v. Erie County (N.Y. App. Div. 1982) — special duty through a 911 call

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D

Facts: Amalia DeLong called 911 to report that a burglar was breaking into her home and gave her address. The call-taker wrote down the wrong address, and the dispatcher sent officers of the Village of Kenmore to an address that did not exist. Concluding the call was a prank, they left.
