Standard procedure required checking the tape of the call to confirm the address; no one did. Relying on the promise of help, she stayed in the house, and minutes later the burglar killed her. A jury found the county and the village liable.

Held: Hancock, J.: as a rule, a government is not liable for failing to provide police protection. But by setting up an emergency number, inviting the public to rely on it, and telling DeLong help was on the way, the government assumed a special duty to her. She relied on the promise, staying home instead of fleeing or seeking help. Failing to follow standard procedures breached that duty. Affirmed.

Why it matters: A special relationship takes the case out of Riss. New York later framed the test (Cuffy v. City of New York, 1987) as all required:
(1) the municipality assumed, through promises or actions, an affirmative duty to act for the injured party;
(2) its agents knew that inaction could lead to harm;
(3) there was direct contact between its agents and the injured party; and
(4) the injured party justifiably relied on the municipality's affirmative undertaking.

cases.name: Taylor v. Olsen
cases.title: Taylor v. Olsen (Or. 1978) — trees beside a highway
cases.html:
main case

Taylor v. Olsen (Or. 1978) — trees beside a highway

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.A

Facts: On a dark, windy January evening, Taylor's car struck a tree that had fallen across a rural highway from Olsen's adjoining timber land. After the accident, the tree was found to be decayed at its center, but nothing on its outside indicated decay. The trial court directed a verdict for Olsen.

Held: Linde, J.: whether a landowner used reasonable care to protect travelers from conditions on the land is usually a jury question. But there must be evidence that a reasonable inspection would have revealed the danger, and there was none: no evidence that boring into an apparently healthy tree is a customary inspection. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Liability for natural conditions depends on what a reasonable inspection would show.

cases.name: Salevan v. Wilmington Park, Inc.
cases.title: Salevan v. Wilmington Park, Inc. (Del. Super. 1950) — baseballs hit into the street
cases.html:
main case

Salevan v. Wilmington Park, Inc. (Del. Super. 1950) — baseballs hit into the street

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.A

Facts: Wilmington Park operated a baseball park next to East Thirtieth Street in Wilmington. Two or three foul balls a game went over the fence onto the street, and the park took only limited precautions. While walking on the street, Salevan was hit by a foul ball. He sued for his injuries.

Held: Wolcott, J.: a landowner whose property adjoins a public street must take reasonable precautions to protect travelers from activities on the land. The park knew balls regularly left the grounds during its 68-game season, so its precautions were inadequate. Judgment for Salevan for $2,500.

Why it matters: A Delaware case. The duty to people outside the land follows the ordinary negligence standard.

cases.name: Sheehan v. St. Paul & Duluth Ry. Co.
cases.title: Sheehan v. St. Paul & Duluth Ry. Co. (7th Cir. 1896) — undiscovered trespassers
cases.html:
main case

Sheehan v. St. Paul & Duluth Ry. Co. (7th Cir. 1896) — undiscovered trespassers

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.B

Facts: Sheehan was walking along the railroad's track, at a place not open to public travel, when his foot slipped and caught in the rails. Before he could free it, a train ran over his foot. The crew did not see him until too late to stop. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad.

Held: Seaman, J.: a possessor owes no duty to anticipate trespassers, who take the land as they find it. The railroad's duty of reasonable care arose only when the crew discovered Sheehan in peril, and there was no evidence they could have stopped after seeing him. Public crossings differ, because their existence gives notice that people will be there. Affirmed.

Why it matters: The duty to a trespasser starts when he is discovered.

cases.name: Barmore v. Elmore
cases.title: Barmore v. Elmore (Ill. App. 1980) — social guests are licensees
cases.html:
main case

Barmore v. Elmore (Ill. App. 1980) — social guests are licensees

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.B

Facts: Barmore and Elmore were officers of the same Masonic lodge. In August 1977, Barmore went to Elmore's home to discuss lodge business. Elmore's adult son, who had a history of mental illness, attacked Barmore with a steak knife. Barmore sued Elmore for failing to protect him from a dangerous condition on the premises. The trial court ruled Barmore a licensee and directed a verdict for Elmore.

Held: Lindberg, J.: Barmore was a licensee, not an invitee, because the visit primarily benefited the lodge, not Elmore. A possessor must warn a licensee only of hidden dangers he knows of. Although the son had a history of mental illness, there was no evidence that Elmore knew or should have known he was likely to attack that night. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Classify the entrant first. A licensee gets a duty to warn only of known dangers.

cases.name: Campbell v. Weathers
cases.title: Campbell v. Weathers (Kan. 1941) — customers who do not buy
cases.html:
main case

Campbell v. Weathers (Kan. 1941) — customers who do not buy

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.B

Facts: Campbell was a regular customer of Weathers's cigar stand and lunch counter. One day he came in, stayed about 15 minutes without buying anything, and then went to use the toilet, which was open to the public. On the way he stepped into an open trap door and was injured. The trial court sustained Weathers's demurrer to the evidence.

Held: Wedell, J.: a regular or prospective customer who enters a place of business open to the public is an invitee, even if he makes no purchase that day. A person who had no intention of becoming a customer, then or later, would not be. Whether Campbell was an invitee was for the jury. Reversed.

Why it matters: The invitation test: a person who enters where the public is invited is an invitee.

cases.name: Whelan v. Van Natta
cases.title: Whelan v. Van Natta (Ky. 1964) — the scope of the invitation
cases.html:
main case

Whelan v. Van Natta (Ky. 1964) — the scope of the invitation

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.B

Facts: Whelan bought some items at Van Natta's grocery and asked for a box. The grocer told him to look in the back room. While searching there, in the dark, he stepped into an unseen stairwell and fell. The trial court entered judgment for Van Natta.

Held: Montgomery, J.: an invitee keeps that status only within the area of the invitation, the part of the premises where the possessor gives reason to believe his presence is desired for the purpose of the visit. Going into the back room for his own purpose (the box), with permission, made Whelan a licensee, owed only a warning of known hidden dangers. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Status can change during a single visit.

cases.name: Rowland v. Christian
cases.title: Rowland v. Christian (Cal. 1968) — abolishing the categories
cases.html:
main case

Rowland v. Christian (Cal. 1968) — abolishing the categories

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.C

Facts: Rowland, a social guest in Christian's apartment, asked to use the bathroom. The porcelain handle of a faucet cracked and broke in his hand, severing tendons and nerves. Christian had known the handle was cracked and had told the building manager, but did not warn Rowland. The trial court granted summary judgment for Christian because a social guest is a licensee who takes the premises as he finds them.

Held: Peters, J.: the status of the entrant as trespasser, licensee, or invitee does not determine the possessor's duty. The test is whether the possessor acted as a reasonable person in managing the property, in view of the probability of injury to others, weighing the Rowland factors. Status may bear on what is reasonable. Christian knew of a concealed danger Rowland was about to encounter and did not warn him, which a jury could find negligent. Reversed.

Why it matters: The leading case rejecting the categories in favor of reasonable care, using the Rowland factors.

Dissent (Burke, J.): the categories developed over many years and give needed certainty. Changing them is for the legislature.

cases.name: Anderson v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.
cases.title: Anderson v. Sears, Roebuck & Co. (E.D. La. 1974) — the elements of personal injury damages
cases.html:
main case

Anderson v. Sears, Roebuck & Co. (E.D. La. 1974) — the elements of personal injury damages

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.A

Facts: A defective heater made by Sears set fire to the Britain family's home. Their infant daughter, Helen, was burned over 40% of her body. She suffered extreme scarring, fingers fused together, and a permanently bent elbow, and faced many costly operations for the rest of her life. The jury awarded her $2,000,000, and Sears moved for a remittitur.

Held: Cassibry, J.: to decide whether an award is excessive, the court examines each element of damages: (1) past physical and mental pain; (2) future physical and mental pain; (3) future medical expenses (here, some 27 projected operations and psychiatric care); (4) loss of earning capacity (she would likely never be self-supporting); and (5) permanent disability and disfigurement. Each element was supported, and the total was not excessive. Motion denied.

Why it matters: This is the framework for valuing a serious personal injury case, element by element.

cases.name: Richardson v. Chapman
cases.title: Richardson v. Chapman (Ill. 1997) — excessive awards and remittitur
cases.html:
main case

Richardson v. Chapman (Ill. 1997) — excessive awards and remittitur

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.A

Facts: Richardson was stopped at a red light when a semi-trailer driven by Chapman hit her car from behind. She became a quadriplegic. The trial court directed a verdict on liability against Chapman and his employer, and the jury awarded Richardson $22,358,814 (and her passenger, McGregor, $102,215). The defendants argued the award was excessive and that her expert's present-value calculations were wrong.

Held: Miller, J.: an award is excessive if it falls outside the range of fair and reasonable compensation, results from passion or prejudice, or shocks the conscience. The jury's award for future medical costs was $1.5 million above the higher of the two figures offered at trial, which unitemized future costs could not explain, so $1 million was remitted. The rest, including large non-economic damages, was within the jury's discretion. Affirmed as modified.

Why it matters: Future economic damages must rest on evidence. Non-economic damages get more deference.

cases.name: Montgomery Ward & Co. v. Anderson
cases.title: Montgomery Ward & Co. v. Anderson (Ark. 1998) — discounts as collateral sources
cases.html:
main case

Montgomery Ward & Co. v. Anderson (Ark. 1998) — discounts as collateral sources

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.B

Facts: Anderson fell in Montgomery Ward's Little Rock store and incurred about $25,000 in hospital bills. Her lawyer negotiated a 50% discount with the hospital. Ward moved to limit her proof to what she actually had to pay and to introduce the discount. The trial court held the discount was a collateral source and allowed evidence of the full bill.

Held: Newbern, J.: gratuitous or discounted medical services are a collateral source and cannot be used to reduce the damages owed by a tortfeasor. The wrongdoer should not benefit from the plaintiff's good fortune, even if she recovers more than her out-of-pocket loss. The rule yields only when collateral-source evidence is relevant for another purpose (such as rebutting a claim of financial need or impeaching testimony). Affirmed.

Why it matters: Courts split on whether the "billed" or the "paid" amount is recoverable when insurers negotiate discounts.

cases.name: Zimmerman v. Ausland
cases.title: Zimmerman v. Ausland (Or. 1973) — refusing surgery and avoidable consequences
cases.html:
main case

Zimmerman v. Ausland (Or. 1973) — refusing surgery and avoidable consequences

Source: Canvas reading (11/10), from the opinion text in the course folder.

Facts: Zimmerman, a substitute teacher, was injured in a car accident. Ausland admitted liability, so only damages were tried. She had a torn semilunar cartilage in her right knee, with swelling and pain after walking, and could no longer join in physical-education games or play volleyball and tennis. Her doctor testified the injury was permanent and would gradually get worse, and that she would "very probably" need surgery to remove the cartilage, after which recovery would be "fairly good." He had prescribed no treatment and said surgery is "not always" required. The defense doctor, who doubted the diagnosis, testified that if she had the tear, routine surgery would let her recover completely. Neither doctor said surgery was called for when he examined her, and no one testified about the operation's risks. The jury was instructed on permanent injury and life-expectancy tables and awarded $7,500. Ausland argued that because routine surgery could cure the injury, and she had a duty to mitigate, it could not be treated as permanent.

Held: Tongue, J.: a plaintiff cannot recover for a permanent injury whose permanence she could have avoided by submitting to treatment, including surgery, that a reasonable person would accept in the same circumstances. The defendant bears the burden of proving an unreasonable failure to mitigate, and the question is ordinarily for the jury. The factors include (1) the risk involved in the operation; (2) its probability of success; and (3) the money or effort required; some courts add the pain involved. Here there was no evidence of the surgery's risk, no evidence that any doctor advised surgery, and no requested instruction on mitigation, so the court could not hold as a matter of law that she had to have surgery. The permanency issue was properly submitted. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Avoidable consequences reduces damages, not liability, and courts are "cautious about insisting that due care requires submission to an operation." It concerns the plaintiff's conduct after the injury; comparative fault (§ 22) concerns her conduct before it.

cases.key: State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Campbell
keys: State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Campbell
cases.name: State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Campbell
cases.title: State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Campbell (U.S. 2003) — ratio and out-of-state conduct
cases.html:
main case

State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Campbell (U.S. 2003) — ratio and out-of-state conduct

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.C

Facts: Campbell, passing six vans on a two-lane highway, caused a crash that killed Ospital and permanently disabled Slusher. State Farm, his insurer, refused offers to settle for the $50,000 policy limits ($25,000 each), assured Campbell his assets were safe, and took the case to trial. The jury returned $185,849 against him, and State Farm at first refused to cover the excess, telling him to put a "For Sale" sign on his house. Campbell then sued State Farm for bad faith, fraud, and IIED. To show a nationwide scheme to cap payouts, he introduced evidence of State Farm's practices across the country over 20 years. The Utah jury awarded $1 million in compensatory damages (reduced from $2.6 million) and $145 million in punitive damages.

Held: Kennedy, J.: the award violated due process under the Gore guideposts. (1) Reprehensibility: State Farm's conduct merited some punishment, but a state may not punish lawful out-of-state conduct or dissimilar conduct unrelated to the plaintiff's harm. (2) Ratio: few awards exceeding a single-digit ratio will satisfy due process, and where compensatory damages are substantial, a 1:1 ratio may be the limit; 145:1 is far beyond it. (3) Comparable penalties: the most relevant civil sanction was a $10,000 fine for fraud. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: This sets the constitutional limit: the single-digit ratio, punishment only for conduct toward this plaintiff, and reprehensibility as the most important guidepost. Philip Morris USA v. Williams (2007) bars punishing for harm to nonparties.

cases.name: Exxon Shipping Co. v. Baker
cases.title: Exxon Shipping Co. v. Baker (U.S. 2008) — maritime cap of 1:1
cases.html:
main case

Exxon Shipping Co. v. Baker (U.S. 2008) — maritime cap of 1:1

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.C

Facts: In 1989 the Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, spilling millions of gallons of crude oil. Its captain, a relapsed alcoholic whom Exxon knew was drinking again, had left the bridge just before the grounding, though he was the only officer licensed to navigate that passage. Exxon paid over $1 billion to settle government environmental claims. Commercial fishermen and Native Alaskans sued for economic losses. The jury awarded $5 billion in punitive damages, which the Ninth Circuit reduced to $2.5 billion. Compensatory damages were about $507.5 million.

Held: Souter, J.: as a matter of federal maritime common law, not constitutional due process, punitive damages for reckless conduct (without intentional or malicious wrongdoing or a profit motive) are limited to a 1:1 ratio with compensatory damages. The chief problem with punitive damages is unpredictability, and studies showed a median ratio below 1:1. Vacated and remanded, effectively reducing the award to about $507.5 million.

Why it matters: The 1:1 ratio is a federal common-law rule for maritime cases. It is not a constitutional limit on the states.

cases.name: Cheatham v. Pohle
cases.title: Cheatham v. Pohle (Ind. 2003) — split-recovery statutes
cases.html:
main case

Cheatham v. Pohle (Ind. 2003) — split-recovery statutes

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.C

Facts: Four years after their divorce, Michael Pohle distributed at least 60 copies of nude photos of his ex-wife, Doris Cheatham, and photos of the two of them having sex, around the small Indiana community where both lived and worked. She sued for invasion of privacy and IIED, and the jury awarded $100,000 in compensatory and $100,000 in punitive damages. Indiana's statute gave the plaintiff only 25% of a punitive award and sent 75% to the state's Violent Crime Victims Compensation Fund. Cheatham challenged the statute as a taking.

Held: Boehm, J.: the statute does not violate the federal or Indiana Takings Clause. Punitive damages are quasi-criminal, serve public purposes, and compensate no one, so a plaintiff has no vested property right in them. The legislature could abolish punitive damages entirely, so it may limit the plaintiff's share. Judgment for the state on the challenge.

Why it matters: Punitive damages are quasi-criminal. Several states use split-recovery statutes or cap punitive awards.

cases.name: Bierczynski v. Rogers
cases.title: Bierczynski v. Rogers (Del. 1968) — concerted action: drag racing
cases.html:
main case

Bierczynski v. Rogers (Del. 1968) — concerted action: drag racing

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.A

Facts: Race and Bierczynski were drag racing side by side on a public highway. Coming over a hill, they saw the Rogerses' car approaching. Race tried to swing back into his lane, lost control, and hit the Rogerses' car at about 70 mph. Bierczynski's car never touched it. The trial court held both racers jointly liable.

Held: Herrmann, J.: participants in a motor vehicle race on a public highway are acting in concert, and each is liable for harm caused by any of them, because each participated in and encouraged the wrongful conduct. Otherwise the victim might be left with only an insolvent defendant, and the driver who happened to collide would bear the whole loss. Affirmed.

Why it matters: A Delaware Supreme Court case. Concert of action makes every participant jointly and severally liable, even one who did not touch the plaintiff.

cases.name: Coney v. J.L.G. Industries, Inc.
cases.title: Coney v. J.L.G. Industries, Inc. (Ill. 1983) — keeping joint and several liability
cases.html:
main case

Coney v. J.L.G. Industries, Inc. (Ill. 1983) — keeping joint and several liability

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.A

Facts: Jasper was killed while operating a hydraulic aerial work platform made by J.L.G. Coney, as administrator of his estate, sued J.L.G. in products liability and negligence. J.L.G. argued that Jasper's employer was partly at fault and that, since Illinois had adopted pure comparative negligence, joint and several liability was abolished and its liability should be reduced by the employer's share. The question was certified to the Illinois Supreme Court.

Held: Moran, J.: adopting comparative negligence does not require abolishing joint and several liability. Comparative negligence reduces the plaintiff's recovery by her own share of fault; it says nothing about relations among defendants. The injury remains indivisible, and the policy that the tortfeasor, not the injured plaintiff, should bear the risk of an insolvent co-defendant still applies. Affirmed and remanded.

Why it matters: The traditional view: the risk of a defendant who cannot pay falls on the other defendants, not the plaintiff.

cases.name: Bartlett v. New Mexico Welding Supply, Inc.
cases.title: Bartlett v. New Mexico Welding Supply, Inc. (N.M. App. 1982) — abolishing joint and several liability
cases.html:
main case

Bartlett v. New Mexico Welding Supply, Inc. (N.M. App. 1982) — abolishing joint and several liability

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.A

Facts: Bartlett was injured in an accident involving a New Mexico Welding vehicle and a third, unidentified car. The jury found Bartlett not negligent, New Mexico Welding 30% responsible, and the unknown driver 70%. Bartlett argued joint and several liability required New Mexico Welding to pay all his damages. The trial court ordered a new trial, and New Mexico Welding took an interlocutory appeal.

Held: Wood, J.: in a pure comparative fault system, joint and several liability among concurrent tortfeasors is abolished. Fault-based apportionment should apply among defendants as it does between plaintiff and defendant, so each defendant pays only its own percentage. New Mexico Welding owed 30%. Reversed.

Why it matters: The several-liability view: fault-based apportionment should run in all directions, and the plaintiff bears the risk of an unknown or insolvent defendant.

cases.name: Bundt v. Embro
cases.title: Bundt v. Embro (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1965) — satisfaction by the state
cases.html:
main case

Bundt v. Embro (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1965) — satisfaction by the state

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.B

Facts: Two cars collided, and passengers sued the owners and drivers of both cars. The passengers had also sued the State of New York in the Court of Claims, for the same accident, and recovered judgments that the state paid. When the defendants learned of this, they moved to amend their answers to plead satisfaction and discharge.

Held: Groat, J.: there is one wrong and one recovery. When a plaintiff receives full satisfaction from one joint tortfeasor, the others are discharged, and it does not matter that the payer was the state, which could only be sued in a different court. Motion granted.

Why it matters: There is one injury and one recovery.

cases.name: Cox v. Pearl Investment Co.
cases.title: Cox v. Pearl Investment Co. (Colo. 1969) — release with reservation
cases.html:
main case

Cox v. Pearl Investment Co. (Colo. 1969) — release with reservation

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.B

Facts: Cox was injured on property owned by Pearl Investment and leased to Goodwill Industries. She settled with Goodwill for $2,500, signing an instrument that expressly reserved her right to sue anyone else who might be liable. When she sued Pearl, Pearl moved for summary judgment under the common-law rule that releasing one joint tortfeasor releases all. The trial court granted it.

Held: Hodges, J.: an instrument that expressly reserves rights against other tortfeasors does not release them. (1) Contract law gives effect to the parties' intent, and Cox plainly did not intend to release Pearl; (2) there is no risk of double recovery, because Pearl gets credit for the $2,500; and (3) the nonsettling tortfeasor is helped, not hurt, by that credit. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: The harsh common-law rule that releasing one released all gives way to the parties' intent.

cases.name: Elbaor v. Smith
cases.title: Elbaor v. Smith (Tex. 1992) — Mary Carter agreements
cases.html:
main case

Elbaor v. Smith (Tex. 1992) — Mary Carter agreements

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.B

Facts: Smith sued three doctors, Elbaor, Syrquin, and Stephens, for malpractice. Syrquin and Stephens entered a "Mary Carter" agreement: they guaranteed Smith $425,010 if she did not recover that much from Elbaor, and she would repay them from any recovery from Elbaor above that amount. They stayed in the case, and at trial their lawyers helped Smith against Elbaor. The jury found Elbaor 88% responsible and awarded $1,872,848 against him.

Held: Gonzalez, J.: Mary Carter agreements are void as against public policy in Texas. They do not promote settlement, since they virtually guarantee a trial against the non-settling defendant, and they distort the trial by aligning supposed adversaries while the jury may not understand the true alignment. Reversed and remanded for a new trial.

Why it matters: A Mary Carter agreement has all required
(1) a settling defendant who stays in the case;
(2) whose liability is reduced in proportion to the plaintiff's recovery from the non-settling defendants; and
(3) whose agreement is often kept secret. Most states allow them with disclosure; Texas and a few others ban them.

Dissent (Doggett, J.): the trial court disclosed the agreements to the jury and protected the adversarial process; so long as genuinely adverse parties remain, the search for truth is not impaired.

cases.name: Knell v. Feltman
cases.title: Knell v. Feltman (D.C. Cir. 1949) — contribution without a joint judgment
cases.html:
main case

Knell v. Feltman (D.C. Cir. 1949) — contribution without a joint judgment

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.C

Facts: Langland, riding as a passenger in her friend Knell's car, was injured when it collided with Feltman's taxi. Because Knell was her friend, she sued only Feltman. Feltman filed a third-party complaint against Knell for contribution. The jury found both negligent.

Held: Miller, J.: when an injury results from the concurrent negligence of two people who did not intend it, one who pays the judgment may obtain contribution from the other, even though the plaintiff did not obtain a joint judgment against both. Letting the plaintiff choose who pays the whole would be unjust and could invite collusion. Feltman could recover half. Affirmed.

Why it matters: The common law barred contribution (Merryweather v. Nixan, 1799). Courts and statutes now allow it among negligent tortfeasors.

cases.name: Yellow Cab Co. of D.C., Inc. v. Dreslin
cases.title: Yellow Cab Co. of D.C., Inc. v. Dreslin (D.C. Cir. 1950) — contribution requires common liability
cases.html:
main case

Yellow Cab Co. of D.C., Inc. v. Dreslin (D.C. Cir. 1950) — contribution requires common liability

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.C

Facts: Mrs. Dreslin was injured in a collision between a Yellow Cab and a car driven by her husband. Both drivers were negligent. She sued Yellow Cab, which cross-claimed against Mr. Dreslin for contribution toward whatever it paid her.

Held: Proctor, J.: under interspousal immunity, the husband was not liable to his wife, so there was no common liability and no right of contribution. Allowing contribution would let the wife's recovery be shifted back to her husband indirectly, undercutting the immunity's purpose of preserving domestic peace. Affirmed.

Why it matters: No liability to the plaintiff means no contribution. With immunities mostly abolished (§ 25), this matters less today.

cases.name: Slocum v. Donahue
cases.title: Slocum v. Donahue (Mass. App. 1998) — good-faith settlement bars contribution
cases.html:
main case

Slocum v. Donahue (Mass. App. 1998) — good-faith settlement bars contribution

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.C

Facts: Donahue was backing his Ford out of his driveway when, he said, the engine raced and the car kept accelerating though he pressed the brake. It crossed the street, hit the curb, went airborne, and hit a fence, killing the Slocums' 18-month-old son. Donahue pleaded guilty to motor vehicle homicide; there was a vodka bottle under his seat. His expert blamed a defective floor mat. The Slocums sued Donahue, who brought in Ford for contribution and indemnity. Before trial, the Slocums settled with Ford for $150,000. The trial court dismissed Donahue's claims against Ford.

Held: Under the Massachusetts contribution statute, a release given in good faith to one tortfeasor discharges it from liability for contribution to others. Donahue showed no collusion or bad faith: the amount was reasonable given the strong case against him, and the Slocums' use of experts Ford had retained was not collusive. Indemnity was unavailable because Donahue was not free of fault. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Settlement bars encourage early settlement. Non-settling defendants get credit for the settlement, and they can challenge only its good faith.

cases.name: Bruckman v. Pena
cases.title: Bruckman v. Pena (Colo. App. 1971) — apportioning successive injuries
cases.html:
main case

Bruckman v. Pena (Colo. App. 1971) — apportioning successive injuries

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.D

Facts: On July 21, 1964, Pena was hurt in a collision caused by Bruckman, who was driving a truck owned by Armored. On June 11, 1965, Pena's injuries were aggravated in a second, unrelated accident. The jury was told to apportion his damages between the defendants and the later tortfeasor, but that "if you find the evidence does not permit such an apportionment, then the defendants are liable for the entire disability." It awarded $50,000.

Held: Dwyer, J.: the plaintiff bears the burden of proving the damages the defendant's negligence caused. It was error to make the first tortfeasor liable for injuries from a later, independent accident just because apportionment is difficult. (A tortfeasor who aggravates a pre-existing condition is liable for the whole, but the reverse does not follow, since the first tortfeasor did not cause the later injury.) Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: Successive, independent injuries are apportioned. The first tortfeasor is liable for later aggravation only if it is a foreseeable result of the first injury, such as negligent medical treatment.

cases.name: Bussard v. Minimed, Inc.
cases.title: Bussard v. Minimed, Inc. (Cal. App. 2003) — going and coming: a risk created at work
cases.html:
main case

Bussard v. Minimed, Inc. (Cal. App. 2003) — going and coming: a risk created at work

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 13.A

Facts: Minimed had its offices sprayed with pesticide overnight. The next morning an employee, Hernandez, became ill from the fumes and left work early, declining to see the company doctor. Driving home, she rear-ended Bussard's car.

Held: The going-and-coming rule does not apply when the employee's commute is affected by a risk arising from the job. The test is foreseeability in the respondeat superior sense: whether the conduct is so startling or unusual that it would be unfair to charge it to the business. Her impairment from workplace fumes was foreseeable. Summary judgment for Minimed was reversed.

Why it matters: Foreseeability here asks whether the risk is typical of the enterprise, not the negligence version of foreseeability.

cases.name: O'Shea v. Welch
cases.title: O'Shea v. Welch (10th Cir. 2003) — frolic and detour
cases.html:
main case

O'Shea v. Welch (10th Cir. 2003) — frolic and detour

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 13.A

Facts: Welch, an Osco Drug store manager, was driving his own car during work hours to Osco's district office to deliver Kansas City Chiefs tickets to other managers, a task done for the company. On a whim, he decided to pull into a service station to get an estimate on his car, turned left across traffic, and hit O'Shea's car. The district court granted summary judgment to Osco on vicarious liability.

Held: McKay, J.: under Kansas law, as predicted, conduct reasonably incidental to the employment and foreseeable to the employer is within its scope. Under the "slight deviation" rule, a detour remains within the scope of employment; a frolic does not. A reasonable jury could find that a brief stop for a car estimate while on a work errand was a slight deviation. Reversed and remanded.

Why it matters: The question is one of degree, so modern courts usually leave frolic and detour to the jury.

cases.name: Murrell v. Goertz
cases.title: Murrell v. Goertz (Okla. App. 1979) — independent contractor
cases.html:
main case

Murrell v. Goertz (Okla. App. 1979) — independent contractor

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 13.B

Facts: Goertz delivered the Oklahoma Publishing Company's newspaper. He got into an argument with a customer, Murrell, and struck her. She sued Goertz and the publisher for assault and battery. Goertz had been hired by an independent distributor that contracted with the publisher; the publisher set general guidelines for delivery but did not supervise how carriers did their work. The trial court granted summary judgment for the publisher.

Held: Reynolds, J.: an independent contractor is one who performs a service for another free from the other's control over the details of the work, except as to the result. The publisher had no direct relationship with Goertz and did not control his manner of delivery; general guidelines about results are not control. It is not vicariously liable. Affirmed.

Why it matters: No vicarious liability for an independent contractor's torts, unless an exception applies.

cases.name: Maloney v. Rath
cases.title: Maloney v. Rath (Cal. 1968) — nondelegable statutory duty
cases.html:
main case

Maloney v. Rath (Cal. 1968) — nondelegable statutory duty

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 13.B

Facts: Rath's car hit Maloney's when its brakes failed. Three months earlier, Rath had had the brakes overhauled by a mechanic, Evanchick, whose negligent work caused the failure. Rath had no reason to know of the defect. The trial court entered judgment for Rath, because an owner is not liable for an independent contractor's negligence.

Held: Traynor, J.: the statutory duty to maintain a car's brakes in good working order is nondelegable. An owner who hires an independent contractor to perform it is liable for the contractor's negligence, though the owner may seek indemnity from the contractor. This is not strict liability for brake failure; it refuses to let the owner shift responsibility to someone who may not be able to pay. Reversed.

Why it matters: Traynor, J.: a nondelegable duty puts the loss on the person who benefits from the activity and can insure against it.

cases.name: Popejoy v. Steinle
cases.title: Popejoy v. Steinle (Wyo. 1991) — no joint enterprise in family errands
cases.html:
note case

Popejoy v. Steinle (Wyo. 1991) — no joint enterprise in family errands

Source: 13th ed. Ch. 13.C (pages the syllabus skims)

Facts: Mrs. Steinle was driving her daughter to buy a calf, which the daughter was to raise as a pet, when she collided with Popejoy's car. The Steinles owned a ranch, but the evidence was that the calf was not for the ranch business. Mrs. Steinle died in the accident. Popejoy, whose injuries first seemed minor, did not file a claim against her estate in time, and later sued Mr. Steinle's estate (he had since died) on the theory that he was vicariously liable as a member of a joint enterprise with his wife. The trial court granted summary judgment.

Held: Golden, J.: a joint enterprise requires (1) an agreement; (2) a common purpose; (3) a community of pecuniary interest; and (4) an equal right of control. The pecuniary-interest element means the enterprise must be commercial and the act must further it. Buying a pet for their daughter was personal, so there was no joint enterprise, and a spouse is not vicariously liable for personal errands. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Joint enterprise is mostly a business doctrine.

cases.name: Malchose v. Kalfell
cases.title: Malchose v. Kalfell (N.D. 2003) — family purpose doctrine
cases.html:
note case

Malchose v. Kalfell (N.D. 2003) — family purpose doctrine

Source: 13th ed. Ch. 13.C (pages the syllabus skims)

Facts: Eric Kalfell, an adult college student living away from home, struck a car driven by Kelly Malchose. She sued Eric for negligence and his parents, Lance and Lisa Kalfell, under the family purpose (family car) doctrine and for negligent entrustment. The parents were the titled owners, Eric listed their ranch as his address, they claimed him as a dependent, and they supported him at college; but Eric had used the car as loan collateral and had moved away. The trial court found Eric negligent and the parents liable under the family car doctrine.

Held: Neumann, J.: the family car doctrine makes a head of household who furnishes a car for a family member's use, pleasure, or business liable for that member's negligent driving. Title is not required, and whether the doctrine applies depends on the totality of the circumstances. The parents' title, financial support, and dependency claim supported the finding, which was not clearly erroneous. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Ownership of record is not required. What matters is who furnished and controlled the car for family use.

cases.name: Smalich v. Westfall
cases.title: Smalich v. Westfall (Pa. 1970) — imputed contributory negligence
cases.html:
note case

Smalich v. Westfall (Pa. 1970) — imputed contributory negligence

Source: 13th ed. Ch. 13.C (pages the syllabus skims)

Facts: Smalich owned a car and was riding in it as a passenger while Westfall drove it with her permission. It collided with a car driven by Blank, and Smalich was killed. Her estate sued both drivers. The jury found for the estate against Blank and found that Westfall's negligence also caused the crash. The trial court entered judgment n.o.v. for Blank, imputing Westfall's negligence to Smalich as the owner.

Held: Eagen, J.: a third person's negligence is imputed to a plaintiff only if their relationship would make the plaintiff vicariously liable as a defendant for that person's negligence. In car cases, only a master-servant relationship or joint enterprise justifies imputation. An owner-passenger ordinarily does not retain control over the details of driving, and the jury found no such control here. Reversed.

Why it matters: The "both ways" test ties imputed contributory negligence to vicarious liability.

Concurrence (Roberts, J.): imputed contributory negligence should be abolished entirely: a passenger cannot safely control a moving car even if he owns it.

cases.name: Sandy v. Bushey
cases.title: Sandy v. Bushey (Me. 1925) — contributory negligence no defense
cases.html:
main case

Sandy v. Bushey (Me. 1925) — contributory negligence no defense

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.A

Facts: Sandy turned his horses out to pasture in a neighbor's field, where Bushey's horse was also pastured. Bushey knew his horse had vicious tendencies. While Sandy was in the pasture feeding his mare, Bushey's horse attacked and kicked him, seriously injuring him. Bushey pleaded Sandy's contributory negligence.

Held: Sturgis, J.: the keeper of a domestic animal known to be vicious is strictly liable as an insurer; the plaintiff need prove only the keeping, the vicious propensity, and the keeper's knowledge (scienter). Because negligence is not the basis of liability, ordinary contributory negligence is no defense. Only a plaintiff who voluntarily and knowingly puts himself in harm's way, or provokes the animal, is barred. Defendant's motion overruled; judgment for Sandy.

Why it matters: Contributory negligence does not bar strict liability, but knowingly encountering the danger does (R2d § 515).

cases.name: Rylands v. Fletcher
cases.title: Rylands v. Fletcher (H.L. 1868) — the origin of strict liability for dangerous land uses
cases.html:
main case

Rylands v. Fletcher (H.L. 1868) — the origin of strict liability for dangerous land uses

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.B

Facts: Rylands, a mill owner, had a reservoir built on his land. The contractors did not seal abandoned mine shafts beneath it, and when the reservoir filled, the water broke through and flooded Fletcher's coal mine nearby. Rylands himself was not negligent. (The case was Fletcher v. Rylands below; the names reversed on appeal.)

Held: Blackburn, J. (Exchequer Chamber): a person who brings onto his land and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes is strictly liable for the damage its escape naturally causes. Lord Cairns (House of Lords) limited this to a "non-natural use" of the land. Judgment for the mine owner.

Why it matters: This is the source of strict liability for abnormally dangerous activities. Non-natural use came to mean an unusual use for the place, not merely something artificial.

cases.name: Miller v. Civil Constructors, Inc.
cases.title: Miller v. Civil Constructors, Inc. (Ill. App. 1995) — firearms are not ultrahazardous
cases.html:
main case

Miller v. Civil Constructors, Inc. (Ill. App. 1995) — firearms are not ultrahazardous

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.B

Facts: Law enforcement officers were holding firearms practice at a gravel pit owned by Civil Constructors. Miller, on nearby property, was struck by a stray bullet that ricocheted out of the pit. He sued the pit's owners, including two counts of strict liability. The trial court dismissed the strict liability counts.

Held: Bowman, J.: discharging firearms is not an ultrahazardous activity. Under the R2d § 520 factors, (1) reasonable care can make it safe, (2) guns are in common use, and (3) firearms practice at a gravel pit is appropriate to the place and has social value, especially for training police. Negligence, not strict liability, governs. Affirmed.

Why it matters: Factor (c), whether reasonable care can eliminate the risk, often decides the case.

cases.name: Indiana Harbor Belt R.R. Co. v. American Cyanamid Co.
cases.title: Indiana Harbor Belt R.R. Co. v. American Cyanamid Co. (7th Cir. 1990) — shipping hazardous chemicals
cases.html:
main case

Indiana Harbor Belt R.R. Co. v. American Cyanamid Co. (7th Cir. 1990) — shipping hazardous chemicals

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.B

Facts: American Cyanamid, a chemical manufacturer, loaded 20,000 gallons of liquid acrylonitrile, a flammable and toxic chemical, into a leased rail tank car bound for New Jersey. At Indiana Harbor Belt's switching yard in suburban Chicago, about 5,000 gallons leaked from a faulty lid or valve. Nearby homes were evacuated, and the railroad spent about $981,000 on cleanup, which state authorities required. It sued the shipper. The district court held the shipper strictly liable.

Held: Posner, J.: shipping acrylonitrile by rail is not abnormally dangerous. Strict liability is for activities whose risks cannot be eliminated by due care, so that the only way to reduce them is to change the activity's level or location. This spill resulted from carelessness, which negligence law can deter. Rerouting hazardous shipments around Chicago's rail hub is impractical, and the shipper did not control the car in transit. The relevant activity is transporting the chemical, not the chemical itself. Reversed and remanded for trial on negligence.

Why it matters: Strict liability is for risks that care cannot prevent. Ask who controls the activity and whether a change in activity level or location is the real solution.

cases.name: Foster v. Preston Mill Co.
cases.title: Foster v. Preston Mill Co. (Wash. 1954) — harm outside the risk
cases.html:
main case

Foster v. Preston Mill Co. (Wash. 1954) — harm outside the risk

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.C

Facts: Foster raised mink on a ranch about two and a quarter miles from where Preston Mill was blasting to build a logging road. Mink are very nervous animals. The blasts frightened the mother mink during whelping season, and they killed their kittens. Foster told the company, which kept blasting. The trial court awarded Foster $1,953.68 on strict liability.

Held: Hamley, J.: strict liability for an ultrahazardous activity covers only harm that results from the risk that makes the activity ultrahazardous, such as debris and concussion. The mink's reaction to noise and vibration came from their exceedingly nervous disposition, not from the normal risks of blasting. Reversed.

Why it matters: The scope limit for strict liability works like proximate cause. Note also the abnormally sensitive activity of the plaintiff.

cases.name: Golden v. Amory
cases.title: Golden v. Amory (Mass. 1952) — act of God
cases.html:
main case

Golden v. Amory (Mass. 1952) — act of God

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.C

Facts: Amory and others owned a hydroelectric plant with a dike along a river. During a hurricane, the river flooded to unprecedented heights, and water overflowed and damaged the Goldens' land. The Goldens sued on strict liability (Rylands) and negligence.

Held: Lummus, J.: the strict liability rule for the escape of stored water does not apply when the escape results from an act of God the owner had no reason to anticipate. The flood was beyond anyone's anticipation, and negligence was not shown. Exceptions overruled; judgment for the defendants.

Why it matters: An unforeseeable force of nature is a defense to strict liability. A foreseeable storm is not.

cases.name: Morgan v. High Penn Oil Co.
cases.title: Morgan v. High Penn Oil Co. (N.C. 1953) — intentional nuisance despite due care
cases.html:
main case

Morgan v. High Penn Oil Co. (N.C. 1953) — intentional nuisance despite due care

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 16.A

Facts: Morgan owned a nine-acre tract with his home, a restaurant, and a trailer park. High Penn built an oil refinery on adjoining land about 1,000 feet from his house. Several days a week the refinery emitted nauseating gases and odors that made people on Morgan's land sick and interfered with their use of it. High Penn kept operating after notice and demand to abate. It argued that its plant was modern and carefully run, so without negligence it could not be liable.

Held: Ervin, J.: a person who intentionally creates or maintains a private nuisance is liable for the resulting injury, regardless of the care or skill used to avoid it. The refinery was a nuisance in fact because of its location and operation, and continuing after notice made the invasion intentional. Negligence is not an element. The court found error on another point and ordered a new trial.

Why it matters: Intentional nuisance does not depend on negligence. Due care is not a defense.

cases.name: Carpenter v. Double R Cattle Co.
cases.title: Carpenter v. Double R Cattle Co. (Idaho 1985) — balancing harm and utility
cases.html:
main case

Carpenter v. Double R Cattle Co. (Idaho 1985) — balancing harm and utility

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 16.A

Facts: Homeowners sued Double R, whose feedlot had expanded to about 9,000 cattle, complaining of manure, odors, flies, and river pollution. The trial court refused instructions based on R2d § 826(b), which allows a nuisance finding when the harm is serious and the defendant could pay damages and still operate, even if the activity's utility outweighs the harm. The jury, told to weigh utility against harm, found for Double R. The court of appeals reversed.

Held: Bakes, J.: Idaho declines to adopt § 826(b). A nuisance is not found where the utility of the activity outweighs the gravity of the harm. People in a developing state must accept some interference for the sake of important industries like cattle feeding. The trial court's instructions were correct. Court of appeals reversed; jury verdict reinstated.

Why it matters: Courts are split on § 826(b), which separates whether the defendant must pay from whether the conduct must stop.

Dissent (Bistline, J.): § 826(b) would require the feedlot to pay for the serious harm it causes without shutting it down; refusing even damages leaves the neighbors without any remedy for a real wrong.

cases.name: Philadelphia Electric Co. v. Hercules, Inc.
cases.title: Philadelphia Electric Co. v. Hercules, Inc. (3d Cir. 1985) — no nuisance claim by a buyer against a seller
cases.html:
note case

Philadelphia Electric Co. v. Hercules, Inc. (3d Cir. 1985) — no nuisance claim by a buyer against a seller

Source: 13th ed. Ch. 16.A

Facts: Pennsylvania Industrial Chemical operated a hydrocarbon resin plant on a site in Chester, Pennsylvania, on the Delaware River. It sold the site to Gould, which later sold it to Philadelphia Electric (PECO). Hercules acquired Pennsylvania Industrial and assumed its liabilities. Resins and chemicals from the old operations were found seeping into the river, and the state required PECO to clean up, at a cost of about $400,000. PECO sued Hercules in private and public nuisance. The jury found for PECO.

Held: Higginbotham, J.: a buyer of land cannot sue the seller in private nuisance. The duty not to maintain a nuisance runs to neighboring owners and occupiers, not to a later buyer of the same land, whose remedies lie in the sale contract under caveat emptor. PECO also could not sue for public nuisance, because it suffered no injury different in kind from the public's (cleanup costs it was ordered to bear are not special injury). Reversed.

Why it matters: Private nuisance protects neighbors. Public nuisance requires special injury (§ 34).

cases.name: Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co.
cases.title: Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co. (N.Y. 1970) — permanent damages instead of an injunction
cases.html:
main case

Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co. (N.Y. 1970) — permanent damages instead of an injunction

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 16.B

Facts: Atlantic Cement built a $45 million cement plant near Albany that employed more than 300 people. Neighbors sued for injunctions and damages, alleging dirt, smoke, and vibration from the plant damaged their property. The trial court found a nuisance but refused an injunction, awarding temporary damages to the time of trial and leaving the neighbors to bring successive suits for later damages.

Held: Bergan, J.: New York's rule was that a nuisance causing substantial damage must be enjoined, even if the defendant's cost of abating far exceeds the harm. But closing the plant would be drastic, and controlling air pollution is a matter for government, not private litigation. The court ordered an injunction that would be vacated once the plant paid permanent damages for the present and future harm to the plaintiffs' land, in effect granting the plant a servitude. Reversed and remanded to set permanent damages.

Why it matters: The defendant can, in effect, buy a servitude to pollute. The dissent (Jasen, J.) said this licenses a continuing wrong and removes the incentive to reduce pollution.

Dissent (Jasen, J.): the majority licenses a continuing wrong; once permanent damages are paid, the incentive to reduce pollution disappears, and the neighbors are forced to accept a servitude for a private party's benefit, a kind of inverse condemnation without public use.

cases.name: Spur Industries, Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co.
cases.title: Spur Industries, Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co. (Ariz. 1972) — compensated injunction
cases.html:
main case

Spur Industries, Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co. (Ariz. 1972) — compensated injunction

Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 16.B

Facts: Spur ran a large cattle feedlot west of Phoenix in an area long devoted to farming. Del Webb bought cheaper farmland nearby and developed Sun City, a retirement community. As it grew, it came within 500 feet of the feedlot, and flies and odor drifted over the homes, discouraging buyers. Webb sued to enjoin the feedlot as a public nuisance. An Arizona statute defined a public nuisance to include a place in a populous area that breeds disease-carrying flies. The trial court enjoined the feedlot but gave Spur no compensation.

Held: Cameron, V.C.J.: (1) the feedlot, lawful when established, had become a public nuisance to the residents of Sun City, who were entitled to relief, so the injunction was proper even though Webb itself "came to the nuisance" and would have been barred if it alone were injured; (2) but because Webb, for profit, brought the people to the nuisance, it must indemnify Spur for a reasonable amount of the cost of moving or shutting down. Affirmed as to the injunction; remanded to fix the indemnity.

Why it matters: The court protected the residents, who had a right to relief, while making the developer who created the conflict pay. This is the "fourth rule" in the table below.
